You are given the following points: A = (10, 12, -16), B = (16, 0, 5), C = (-6, -8, 12).

Which point is closest to the yz-plane?
?
A
B
C
What is the distance from the yz-plane to this point?

Which point is farthest from the xy-plane?
?
A
B
C
What is the distance from the xy-plane to this point?

Which point lies on the xz-plane?
?
A
B
C

solution.p: SOLUTION
The distance from a point to the yz-plane is the absolute value of the x-coordinate.
The point C(-6,-8,12) has the x coordinate with the smallest absolute value, so C is the point closest to the yz- plane.
The distance from the yz-plane to C is given by the absolute value of the x-coordinate, i.e. \left| -6 \right| = 6.
The distance from a point to the xy-plane is the absolute value of the z-coordinate.
The point A(10,12,-16) has the z coordinate with the largest absolute value, so A is the point farthest from the xy- plane.
The distance from the xy-plane to A is given by the absolute value of the z-coordinate, i.e. \left| -16 \right| = 16.
A point lies on the xz-plane if its y-coordinate is zero. Thus B(16,0,5) lies on the xz-plane.

Resolve the following vectors into components:
(a) The vector \vec v in 2-space of length 7 pointing up at an angle of 3\pi/4 measured from the positive x-axis.
\vec v = \vec i + \vec j
(b) The vector \vec w in 3-space of length 5 lying in the yz-plane pointing upward at an angle of 2\pi/3 measured from the positive y-axis.
\vec v = \vec i + \vec j + \vec k

static.solution:
(a) The components are v_1 = 7 \cos 3\pi/4 = (7)(-{1\over\sqrt 2}) = -{7 \over\sqrt 2} and v_2 = 7 \sin 3\pi/4 = (7)({1\over\sqrt 2}) = {7 \over\sqrt 2}. Thus \vec v = -{7 \over\sqrt 2}\,\vec i + {7 \over\sqrt 2}\,\vec j.
(b) Since the vector lies in the yz-plane, its x-component is 0. Its y-component is (5)(\cos 2\pi/3) = -{5 \over 2}, and and its z-component is (5)(\sin 2\pi/3) = {5\sqrt 3 \over 2}. So the vector is \vec w = -{5 \over 2}\,\vec j + {5\sqrt 3 \over 2}\,\vec k.

statement.p: (a) Find a unit vector from the point P=(2,1) and toward the point Q=(10,16).
(b) Find a vector of length 51 pointing in the same direction.

static.solution:
(a) The displacement from P to Q is given by \overrightarrow{PQ} = (10\,\vec i + 16\,\vec j) - (2\,\vec i + 1\,\vec j) = 8\,\mathit{\vec i}+15\,\mathit{\vec j}. Since \mbox{len}{\overrightarrow{PQ}} = \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = 17, a unit vector \vec u in the direction of \overrightarrow{PQ} is given by \vec u = \frac{1}{17}\,\overrightarrow{PQ} = \frac{1}{17}\,(8\,\mathit{\vec i}+15\,\mathit{\vec j}) .
(b) A vector of length 51 pointing in the same direction is given by 51\,\vec u = \frac{51}{17}\,(8\,\mathit{\vec i}+15\,\mathit{\vec j}) = 24\,\mathit{\vec i}+45\,\mathit{\vec j}.

solution.p: Vectors are parallel if they are scalar multiples of one another. If we multiply \langle 0.99,-0.12 \rangle by any scalar, it will change its length, making it no longer a unit vector, unless the scalar we choose is 1 or -1. Multiplying by 1 gives us the same vector again, but we were asked for a different one. Thus we must choose -1\cdot\langle 0.99,-0.12 \rangle, which is \langle -0.99,0.12 \rangle.

Consider the wind velocity vectors \vec w_1 = 3\mathit{\vec i}-\mathit{\vec j} \qquad \vec w_2 = -\mathit{\vec i}-3\mathit{\vec j} \qquad \vec w_3 = \mathit{\vec i}+6\mathit{\vec j} \vec w_4 = -8\mathit{\vec i}+2\mathit{\vec j} \qquad \vec w_5 = -4\mathit{\vec i}-\mathit{\vec j}.
Which of the wind velocity vectors increases the plane's speed the most?

Wind

w1
w2
w3
w4
w5

Wind
?
w1
w2
w3

static.solution:
\vec w in the direction of the airplane. A direction vector for the airplane is \vec v = -\mathit{\vec i}-\mathit{\vec j}. The component of \vec w_1 in the direction of \vec v is given by {{\vec w_1 \cdot \vec v} \over ||{\vec v}}|| = {-2 \over \sqrt{2}} \approx -1.41.
Similarly, we find the component for each wind vector in the direction of the airplane. We see that, in the direction of the airplane, the component of \vec w_1 is -1.41, of \vec w_2 is 2.83, of \vec w_3 is -4.95, of \vec w_4 is 4.24, and of \vec w_5 is 3.54.
Thus, the vector \vec w_4 increases the plane's speed the most and the vector \vec w_3 slows the plane down the most.

angle =

solution.p: Let A be one corner of the base, B be the opposite corner on the base, and C be the point that is directly above B on the top of the box. ABC is a right triangle with right angle at B, and AC is its hypotenuse. AC is also a diagonal of the box, and AB is a diagonal of the base of the box. Therefore angle A of this triangle is the angle that we want.

Its cosine is \displaystyle{\begin{aligned} \cos(A) \amp = \frac{\text{length of }AB}{\text{length of }AC} \\ \amp = \frac{\sqrt{18^2+7^2}}{\sqrt{18^2+7^2+4^2}} \end{aligned} } so \displaystyle{A = \arccos\left(\frac{\sqrt{18^2+7^2}}{\sqrt{18^2+7^2+4^2}}\right) \approx {0.204225} \text{ radians}}.

statement.p: The force on an object is \vec F = -22\,\mathit{\vec j}. For the vector \vec v = -3\,\mathit{\vec i}-\,\mathit{\vec j}, find:
(a) The component of \vec F parallel to \vec v:
(b) The component of \vec F perpendicular to \vec v:
The work, W, done by force \vec F through displacement \vec v:

static.solution:
\vec v. Since ||\vec v|| = \sqrt{(-3)^2+(-1)^2} = \sqrt{10}, the unit vector in direction of \vec v is \vec u = \vec v/\sqrt{10}. Then
(a) \vec F_{||} = (\vec F \cdot \vec u) \vec u = (22/\sqrt{10}) \vec u = \frac{-66}{10} \vec i + \frac{-22}{10} \vec j.
(b) We have \vec F_{\perp} = \vec F - \vec F_{||} = (-22\,\mathit{\vec j}) - (\frac{-66}{10} \vec i + \frac{-22}{10} \vec j) \approx 6.6\,\mathit{\vec i}-19.8\,\mathit{\vec j}.
(c) Since work is the dot product of the force and displacement vectors, we have W = \vec F \cdot \vec v = 22.

statement.p: Consider the vectors \vec a = 2\,\mathit{\vec i}+\,\mathit{\vec j}-\,\mathit{\vec k}, \qquad \vec b = - \vec{i} - 2 \vec{j} + \vec{k}, \qquad \vec c = -2\,\mathit{\vec i}-\,\mathit{\vec j}+\,\mathit{\vec k} \vec d = \,\mathit{\vec i}+\,\mathit{\vec j}+3\,\mathit{\vec k},\qquad \vec g = \,\mathit{\vec i}+2\,\mathit{\vec j}-\,\mathit{\vec k}. Which pairs (if any) of these vectors are
(a) Are perpendicular?

p.em: (Enter none or a pair or list of pairs, e.g., if \vec a is perpendicular to \vec b and \vec c, enter (a,b),(a,c).)

statement.p: (b) Are parallel?

p.em: (Enter none or a pair or list of pairs, e.g., if \vec a is parallel to \vec b and \vec c, enter (a,b),(a,c).)

statement.p: (c) Have an angles less than \pi/2 between them?

p.em: (Enter none or a pair or list of pairs, e.g., if \vec a is at an angle less than pi/2 from \vec b and \vec c, enter (a,b),(a,c).)

statement.p: (d) Have an angle of more than \pi/2 between them?

p.em: (Enter none or a pair or list of pairs, e.g., if \vec a is at an angle greater than pi/2 from \vec b and \vec c, enter (a,b),(a,c).)

static.solution:
(a) Perpendicular vectors have a dot product of 0. Since \vec a\cdot\vec d = (2)\cdot(1) + (1)\cdot(1) + (-1)\cdot(3) = 0 and similarly \vec b\cdot\vec d = 0, \vec c\cdot\vec d = 0, \vec d\cdot\vec g = 0, the pairs we want are (\vec a, \vec d), (\vec b, \vec d), (\vec c, \vec d), (\vec d, \vec g).
(b) Parallel vectors are multiples of one another. Since \vec a and \vec c are constant multiples of each other and similarly for \vec b and \vec g, the pairs we want are (\vec a, \vec c), (\vec b, \vec g).
(c) Since \vec v\cdot\vec w= \Vert\vec v\Vert \Vert\vec w\Vert\cos\theta, the dot product of the vectors we want is positive. Since \vec a\cdot\vec g = (2)\cdot(1) + (1)\cdot(2) + (-1)\cdot(-1) > 0 and similarly \vec b\cdot\vec c > 0, the pairs we want are (\vec a, \vec g), (\vec b, \vec c).
(d) Vectors with an angle of more than \pi/2 between them have a negative dot product. Since \vec a\cdot\vec b = (2)\cdot(-1) + (1)\cdot(-2) + (-1)\cdot(1) \lt 0 and similarly \vec a\cdot\vec c \lt 0, \vec b\cdot\vec g \lt 0, \vec c\cdot\vec g \lt 0, the pairs we want are (\vec a, \vec b), (\vec a, \vec c), (\vec b, \vec g), (\vec c, \vec g).

p.m: \text{the paths cross, and the particles collide there}

static.solution:
(2,-4,5) in the direction of the vector \vec i + 2 \vec j - 2 \vec k and the second passes through (-8,-9,10) in the direction of the vector 3 \vec i + 3 \vec j - 3 \vec k. The two paths are not parallel.
Is there a time t when the two particles are at the same place at the same time? If so, then the particles collide, and their coordinates will be the same. Equating coordinates, we get 2 + t = -8 + 3 t, \quad -4 + 2 t = -9 + 3 t,\quad 5 - 2 t = 10 - 3 t.
Since all three equations are solved by t=5, the two particles do in fact arrive at the same place at the same time, and so they do collide.
Then, the two paths cross if there are times t_1 and t_2 such that the position of the first particle at time t_1 is the same as the position of the second particle at time t_2. In this case this is obvious: when t_1 = t_2 = 5, the paths cross.

equation:

static.solution: Both lines are parallel to the x-axis; thus our plane must have x-slope zero. On the other hand, the line in the xy-plane is 6 units down and unit in front of of the line in the y z-plane; hence the y-slope of our plane must be -2. Thus the equation is z = 0 x - 2 y + c, for some constant c. Since the plane contains the point (0,0,6), the value of c must be 6. So the equation is z = -2 y + 6. This is shown in the graph below.

statement.p: (a) Find a vector parallel to the line of intersection of the planes x - y - 2 z = 4 and 5 x - 5 y - 2 z = 12.
(b) Show that the point \left(1,-1,-1\right) lies on both planes. Then find a vector parametric equation for the line of intersection.

static.solution:
(a) Normal vectors to the two planes are \vec n_1 = \vec i - \vec j - 2 \vec k \quad \hbox{ and } \quad \vec n_2 = 5\vec i - 5 \vec j - 2 \vec k. The vector \vec n_1\times\vec n_2 is perpendicular to both planes and parallel to the line of intersection: \vec n_1\times\vec n_2 = \left| \begin{array}{ccc} \vec i \amp \vec j \amp \vec k\\ 1 \amp -1 \amp -2\\ 5 \amp -5 \amp -2 \end{array} \right| = -8\,\mathit{\vec i}-8\,\mathit{\vec j}.
(b) To check that the point \left(1,-1,-1\right) lies on the planes, substitute into each equation. x - y - 2 z = (1)(1) + (-1)(-1) + (-2)(-1) = 4, and 5 x - 5 y - 2 z = (5)(1) + (-5)(-1) + (-2)(-1) = 12. Thus, the point lies on both planes. Then a vector parametric equation of the line is \vec r(t) = \left(1-8t\right)\,\mathit{\vec i}-\left(1+8t\right)\,\mathit{\vec j}-\,\mathit{\vec k}.

statement.p: Evaluate the surface integral \int_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \ d \mathbf{S} where \mathbf{F}=5xy\boldsymbol{i}+6x^{2}\boldsymbol{j}+5yz\boldsymbol{k}\ and S is the surface z=xe^y,\ 0 \le x \le 1, 0 \le y \le 1, with upwards orientation.

static.solution: \mathbf{r}(x,y)=(x,y,g(x,y)) where z = g(x,y) = xe^y and D is the square D = [0,1]\times [0,1]. S has upwards orientation, so \int_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \ d \mathbf{S} = \int\int_D ( -5 x y \frac{\delta g}{\delta x} - 6 x^2 \frac{\delta g}{\delta y} + 5 y z)\ dA = \int\int_D (-5 x y e^y - 6 x^3 e^y + 5 y z)\ dA = \int_0^1\int_0^1 (-5 x y e^y - 6 x^3 e^y + 5 x y e^y)\ dy\ dx = \int_0^1 [- 6 x^3 e^y]_0^1\ dx = \int_0^1 - 6 x^3 (e - 1)\ dx = 6(1 - e)\int_0^1 x^3 \ dx = \frac {3} 2 (1-e)

statement.p: Find a vector \mathbf{n} normal to the plane with the equation 5x+5y+z=7.
\mathbf{n} = \left\lt 5 ,\right., \left.\right>
Find an equation of the plane through the three points given:

static.solution:
\mathbf{n}\cdot \left\lt x,y,z\right>=d
To find the normal vector to the plane, \mathbf{n}, we first compute the vectors \vec{PQ} and \vec{PR} that lie in the plane, and then find the cross product of these vectors. This gives:
\vec{PQ}= \left\lt 4,4,-1\right> - \left\lt 0,0,1\right> = \left\lt 4,4,-2\right>
\vec{PR}= \left\lt -2,1,-2\right> - \left\lt 0,0,1\right> = \left\lt -2,1,-3\right>
\mathbf{n} = \vec{PQ}\times \vec{PR} = \left| \begin{array}{ccc} \boldsymbol{i} \amp \boldsymbol{j} \amp \boldsymbol{k} \\ 4 \amp 4 \amp -2 \\ -2 \amp 1 \amp -3 \end{array} \right|
\qquad = \left| \begin{array}{cc} 4 \amp -2 \\ 1 \amp -3 \end{array} \right| \boldsymbol{i} -\left| \begin{array}{cc} 4 \amp -2 \\ -2 \amp -3 \end{array} \right| \boldsymbol{j} +\left| \begin{array}{cc} 4 \amp 4 \\ -2 \amp 1 \end{array} \right| \boldsymbol{k}
\qquad =-10 \boldsymbol{i} + 16 \boldsymbol{j} + 12 \boldsymbol{k}
We now choose any of the three points in the plane, say P=\left(0,0,1\right), and compute d.
d=\mathbf{n} \cdot\vec{OP}=\left\lt -10,16,12\right> \cdot \left\lt 0,0,1\right> = 12
Finally we obtain the following equation of the plane:
-10 x + 16 y + 12 z = 12.

statement.p: Find the equation of the ellipsoid passing through the points (\pm 2,0,0),(0,\pm 1,0) and (0,0,\pm 2)
Find the equation of the hyperboloid of one sheet passing through the points (\pm 3,0,0),(0,\pm 7,0) and (\pm 6,0,5),(0,\pm 14,5)

static.solution:
z=z_{0} are ellipses. Hence, the equation of the hyperboloid has the form
\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^2-\left(\frac{z}{c}\right)^2=1
Substituting z=0 we get
\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{b}\right)^2=1
By the given information this ellipse has x and y intercepts at the points (\pm 3,0),(0,\pm 7). So we get
\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{7}\right)^2-\left(\frac{z}{c}\right)^2=1
Substituting z=5 we get
\frac{x^2}{3^2} + \frac{y^2}{7^2} -\frac{5^2}{c^2}=1
\frac{x^2}{9} + \frac{y^2}{49} =1+\frac{25}{c^2}=\frac{c^2+25}{c^2}
\frac{c^2 x^2}{9(c^2+25)} + \frac{c^2 y^2}{49(c^2+25)} = 1
\left(\frac{x}{\frac{3}{c}\sqrt{c^2+25}}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{\frac{7}{c}\sqrt{c^2+25}}\right)^2=1
By the given information the following must hold: \frac{3}{c}\sqrt{c^2+25}=6 and \frac{7}{c}\sqrt{c^2+25}=14
\frac{\sqrt{c^2+25}}{c}=2, so c^2+25=4c^2 and 3c^2=25
Thus, c=\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}, and by substituting we obtain the following equation
\left(\frac{x}{3}\right)^2 +\left(\frac{y}{7}\right)^2-\left(\frac{z}{\frac{5}{\sqrt{3}}}\right)^2=1

solution.p: SOLUTION
1. Completing the squares, yields (x-2)^2+(y-2)^2+(z-1)^2 = \frac{1}{4}. Thus the sphere is centered at (2,2,1) and has radius \frac{1}{2}. Its graph matches D.
2. The sphere is centered at (0,0,-1) and has radius \frac{3}{2}. Thus it matches C.
3. Completing the squares, yields (x-1)^2+(y+1)^2+(z-1)^2 = 1. Thus the sphere is centered at (1,-1,1) and has radius 1. Its graph matches E.
4. The sphere is centered at the origin and it has radius 2. Thus it matches A.

static.solution:
\left( \frac{x}{a} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{y}{b} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{z}{c} \right)^2=1, for a=5, b=4, c=1.
To find the trace obtained by intersecting the ellipsoid with the plane z=2, we set z=2 in the equation of the ellipsoid. This gives
\left( \frac{x}{5} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{y}{4} \right)^2 + 2^2=1
\left( \frac{x}{5} \right)^2 + \left( \frac{y}{4} \right)^2=-3
We conclude that the trace is an empty set.

statement.p: Convert from rectangular to polar coordinates:
Note: Choose r and \theta such that r is nonnegative and 0 \leq \theta \lt 2\pi
\mathbf{(a)}\quad (1,0)\quad\Rightarrow_{(r,\theta)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(b)}\quad(18,\frac{18}{\sqrt{3}})\quad\Rightarrow_{(r,\theta)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(c)}\quad(-7,7)\quad\Rightarrow_{(r,\theta)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(d)}\quad(-1,\sqrt{3})\quad\Rightarrow_{(r,\theta)}\quad(,)

static.solution:
\mathbf{(a)} The point (1,0) is on the positive x axis distanced 1 units from the origin. Hence, r=1 and \theta=0.
Thus, (r,\theta)=(1,0)
\mathbf{(b)} The point (18,\frac{18}{\sqrt{3}}) is in the first quadrant so \theta = \tan^{-1} \left(\frac{\frac{18}{\sqrt{3}}}{18}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}.
Also, r=\sqrt{{18}^2+\left({\frac{18}{\sqrt{3}}}\right)^2} = \sqrt{432} Hence, (r,\theta)=\left(\sqrt{432},\frac{\pi}{6}\right)
\mathbf{(c)} The point (-7,7) is in the second quadrant. Hence, { \theta ={ \tan}^{-1}\left(\frac{7}{-7}\right) = {\tan}^{-1}(-1)=\pi -\frac{\pi }{4}=\frac{3\pi }{4}}. Also, r=\sqrt{{(-7)}^{2}+{7}^{2}}=\sqrt{98}. Hence, \left(r,\theta\right)=\left(\sqrt{98},\frac{3\pi }{4}\right).
\mathbf{(d)} The point \left(-1,\sqrt{3}\right) is in the second quadrant, hence, \theta ={\tan}^{-1}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{-1}\right)= \tan^{-1}\left(-\sqrt{3}\right)=\pi -\frac{\pi }{3}=\frac{2\pi }{3}. Also, r=\sqrt{\left(-1\right)^{2}+{\left(\sqrt{3}\right)}^{2}}=\sqrt{4}=2. Hence, \left(r,\theta \right)=\left(2,\frac{2\pi }{3}\right).

statement.p: Convert from polar to rectangular coordinates:
\mathbf{(a)}\quad(2,\frac{3\pi}{2})\quad\Rightarrow_{(x,y)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(b)}\quad(6,\frac{\pi}{2})\quad\Rightarrow_{(x,y)}\quad(,)
\mathbf{(c)}\quad(3,0)\quad\Rightarrow_{(x,y)}\quad(,)

static.solution:
\mathbf{(a)} Since r=2 and \theta =\frac{3\pi}{2}, we have: x=r\cos\theta=2\cos \frac{3\pi}{2}=2\cdot 0=0 y=r\sin\theta=2\sin \frac{3\pi}{2}=2\cdot -1=-2 \Downarrow (x,y)=(0,-2)
\mathbf{(b)} For (6,\frac{\pi}{2}) we have r=6 and \theta=\frac{\pi}{2}. Hence, x=r\cos\theta=6\cos \frac{\pi}{2}=6\cdot 0=0 y=r\sin\theta=6\sin \frac{\pi}{2}=6\cdot 1=6 \Downarrow (x,y)=(0,6)
\mathbf{(c)} Since r=3 and \theta =0, we have: x=r\cos\theta=3\cos 0=3\cdot 1=3 y=r\sin\theta=3\sin 0=3\cdot 0=0 \Downarrow (x,y)=(3,0)

statement.p: Which of the following two equations defines a horizontal line?
Write "T" if the equation defines a horizontal line, "F" otherwise.

static.solution:
r=8 \csc \theta is the polar equation of a horizontal line, as it can be written as r=8/\sin \theta, so r \sin \theta = 8, which becomes y=8.
On the other hand, the equation r=8 \sec \theta is the polar equation of a vertical line, as it can be written as r=8/\cos \theta, so r \cos \theta = 8, which becomes x=8.

statement.p: The following polar equation describes a circle in rectangular coordinates: r = 10\cos\theta Locate its center on the xy-plane, and find the circle's radius.

static.solution: r and substituting x =r \cos \theta and {r}^{2}={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} gives {r}^{2}=10 r \cos \theta \Rightarrow {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=10 x We complete the square to obtain {x}^{2} - 10 x +{y}^{2}=0 \left(x - 5\right)^{2} + y^2 = {5}^{2} Thus, r=10 \cos \theta is the equation of a circle of radius 5 and center \left(5,0\right).

Convert the following point from rectangular to cylindrical coordinates: (-2,-2\sqrt{3},-2).
Usage: To enter a point, for example (x,y,z), type "(x, y, z)".

static.solution:
(x,y,z)=(-2,-2\sqrt{3},-2). We first find r: r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\sqrt{(-2)^2+(-2\sqrt{3})^2}=4. Since the point (x,y)=(-2,-2\sqrt{3}) lies in the third quadrant, \pi\leq \theta\leq \frac{3\pi}{2}. Hence \tan \theta=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{-2\sqrt{3}}{-2}=\sqrt{3}, so \theta=\frac{4 \pi}{3}.
The cylindrical coordinates are thus (r,\theta,z)=\left( 4, \frac{4 \pi}{3}, -2 \right).

statement.p: Convert the following point from spherical to rectangular coordinates: \left(3, \frac{7 \pi}{6}, \frac{7 \pi}{4}\right).
Usage: To enter a point, for example (x,y,z), type "(x, y, z)".
Convert the following point from rectangular to spherical coordinates: \left(\frac{ 3\sqrt{3}}{4},\frac{- 9}{4},\frac{ 3}{2}\right).
Usage: To enter a point, for example (x,y,z), type "(x, y, z)".

static.solution:
x=\frac{ 3\sqrt{3}}{4}, y=\frac{- 9}{4}, and z=\frac{ 3}{2}. The radial coordinate is \rho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}=\sqrt{\textstyle \left(\frac{ 3\sqrt{3}}{4}\right)^2+\left(\frac{- 9}{4}\right)^2+\left(\frac{ 3}{2}\right)^2}=3. The angular coordinate \theta satisfies \tan \theta=\frac{y}{x}=\frac{- 9/4}{ 3\sqrt{3}/4}=-\sqrt{3} so either \theta=\frac{2 \pi}{3} or \theta=\frac{5 \pi}{3}. Since the point (x,y)=(\frac{ 3\sqrt{3}}{4},\frac{- 9}{4}) is in the fourth quadrant, the correct choice is \theta=\frac{5 \pi}{3}. The angle of declination \phi satisfies \cos \phi=\frac{z}{\rho}=\frac{ \sqrt{1}}{2}, \qquad 0\leq \phi\leq \pi and so \phi=\frac{ \pi}{3}.
The spherical coordinates are thus (\rho,\theta,\phi)=\left(3,\frac{5 \pi}{3},\frac{ \pi}{3}\right).

static.solution:
(\theta,\phi) for Cape Town. Since it's longitude lies to the east of Greenwich, that is, in the positive \theta direction, \theta=18.3667^{\circ}. The latitude is south of the equator, hence \phi=90^{\circ}+33.9167^{\circ}=123.917^{\circ}.
We now use the formulas of x, y, and z in terms of \rho, \theta, and \phi to find the rectangular coordinates: \begin{array}{rcl} x \amp =\amp \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta=6367\sin123.917^{\circ}\cos18.3667^{\circ}= 5014.48 \\ y \amp =\amp \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta=6367\sin123.917^{\circ}\sin18.3667^{\circ}= 1664.86 \\ z \amp =\amp \rho\cos\phi = 6367\cos123.917^{\circ}= -3552.73 \end{array}

li.p: The parametric curve x = (3t+4)^2, y = 5(3t+4)^2-9, for 0 \leq t \leq 3 is a line segment.

A parametrization of the graph of y = \ln(x) for x > 0 is given by x = e^t, y = t for -\infty \lt t \lt \infty.

solution.p: SOLUTION
1. Eliminating the parameter t yields the equation y = 5x -9,\; 16 \le x \le 169. Thus the parametric curve is a line segment and the statement is True.
2. The direction vector of the line is \langle 0, 5, 1\rangle. This vector is not parallel to the x-axis. Thus the statement is False.
3. Substituting x = e^t, y = t into the equation y= \ln(x) yields t = \ln(e^t) = t. For the given values of t, x > 0. Thus the statement is True.

statement.p: Find a parameterization (x(t),y(t),z(t)) for the curve y = 2-x^{3} that is parallel to the xy-plane. Your parametrized curve should pass through the point (0, 2 , 1) when t = 1, and have x'(1)\neq 0.

static.solution: z is constant since the curve is parallel to the xy-plane, so z=1 since it passes through (0,2,1). One possible answer is x = t-1, \quad y = 2-\left(t-1\right)^{3}, \quad z=1, which passes through the indicated point, with x'(1)=1.

statement.p: A particle moves on a circle of radius 5 cm, centered at the origin, in the xy-plane (x and y measured in centimeters). At time t=0 it starts at the point (0,5) and moves counterclockwise as t increases, going once around the circle in 10 seconds at constant speed.
(a) Write a parameterization for the particle's motion.
(b) What is the particle's speed?
speed =

p.em: (Give .)

static.solution:
(a) For any positive constant k, the parameterization x=-5\sin(kt)\quad y=5\cos(kt) moves counterclockwise on a circle of radius 5 starting at the point (0,5). We choose k to make the period 10 seconds. If k\cdot 10=2\pi, then k=\pi/5 and the parameterization is x=-5\sin\left(\frac {\pi t}{5}\right)\qquad y=5\cos \left(\frac {\pi t}{5}\right).
(b) Since it takes 10 seconds for the particle to go around the circle \mbox{Speed}=\frac{\mbox{Circumference of circle}}{10} = \frac {2\pi(5)}{10} = \frac {\pi}{1}\mbox{ cm/sec}.

statement.p: Suppose a curve is traced by the parametric equations x = 4 \big(\sin(t)+\cos(t)\big)
as t runs from 0 to \pi. At what point (x,y) on this curve is the tangent line horizontal?

static.solution:
0 = \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} = \frac{12\cdot 2\cos(t)\sin(t) - 24\cos(t)}{4 \big(\cos(t)-\sin(t)\big)}.
If this fraction is zero then its numerator is zero 0=dy/dt = 24\cos(t)\big(\sin(t)-1\big) so \cos(t)=0 or \sin(t)=1. Since 0\leq t \leq \pi it follows that t = \frac{\pi}{2} is the only possibility. It works because the denominator of the fraction \displaystyle \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dy/dt}{dx/dt} is not zero when t=\pi/2, so there really is a horizontal tangent when t=\pi/2.
Plug t=\pi/2 into the parametric equations to obtain x,y-coordinates of the point where the horizontal line is tangent x= 4 \left(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\right)= 4 and y = 32 - 12\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) - 24\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 32 - 0 - 24 = 8.

statement.p: Determine whether {\bf r}_1 and {\bf r}_2 collide or intersect:

The two paths
collide
do not collide

The two paths
do not intersect
intersect

static.solution:
t such that:

Equating corresponding components we obtain the following equations:
t=t+4.5
t^2=16t^{2}
t^3=216
The second equation implies that t=0, but this value does not satisfy the other equations. Therefore, the equations have no solution, which means that the paths do not collide.
The two paths intersect if there exist values of t and s such that:
\left\lt s,s^2,s^3 \right> = \left\lt t+4.5, 16t^{2},216 \right>
Or equivalently:
s=t+4.5
s^2=16t^{2}
s^3=216
The second equation implies that s=\pm 4 t, and the third equation implies s=6. Hence t=\pm 1.5
We can see that one of the solutions satisfies the first equation, hence the two paths intersect.

A child wanders slowly down a circular staircase from the top of a tower. With x,y,z in feet and the origin at the base of the tower, her position t minutes from the start is given by x=30\cos t,\quad y = 30 \sin t, \quad z = 110 - 5 t.
(a) How tall is the tower?
height = ft
(b) When does the child reach the bottom?
time = minutes
(c) What is her speed at time t?
speed = ft/min
(d) What is her acceleration at time t?
acceleration = ft/min{}^2

static.solution:
(a) Since z=110 feet when t=0, the tower is 110 feet high.
(b) The child reaches the bottom when z=0, so t=110/5=22 minutes.
(c) Her velocity is given by \vec v =\frac{d\vec r}{dt} = -(30\sin t)\vec i +(30\cos t)\vec j - 5\vec k, so \hbox{Speed} = ||\vec v|| = \sqrt{(-30\sin t)^2+(30\cos t)^2 + (-5)^2} = \sqrt{30^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{925} \mbox{ ft/min}.
(c) Her acceleration is given by \vec a = \frac{d\vec v}{dt} = -(30 \cos t)\vec i -(30 \sin t)\vec j \mbox{ ft/min}^2.

Usage: To enter a vector, for example \langle x,y,z\rangle, type \lt x, y, z \gt

static.solution: \mathbf{a}(t) to obtain the velocity vector: \mathbf{v}(t) = \int_0^t \left\lt u,9\right> du = \left.\left\langle \frac{u^2}{2},9 u\right\rangle\right|_0^t+\mathbf{v}_0 = \left\langle \frac{t^2}{2},9 t\right\rangle+\mathbf{v}_0. The initial condition \mathbf{v}(0)=\left\lt 3,-2\right> gives: \mathbf{v}(0) = \langle 0,0\rangle+\mathbf{v}_0=\left\lt 3,-2\right> so \mathbf{v}_0=\left\lt 3,-2\right> and we obtain \mathbf{v}(t) = \left\langle \frac{t^2}{2},9 t\right\rangle+\left\lt 3,-2\right> = \left\langle \frac{t^2}{2}+3,9 t - 2\right\rangle. We now integrate the velocity vector to find \mathbf{r}(t): \begin{array}{rcl} \mathbf{r}(t) \amp =\amp \displaystyle\int_0^t \left\langle \frac{u^2}{2}+3,9 u - 2\right\rangle\ du \\ \amp =\amp \left.\left\langle \frac{u^3}{6}+3 u,\frac{9 u^2}{2} - 2 u\right\rangle\right|_0^t +\mathbf{r}_0 \\ \amp =\amp \left\langle \frac{t^3}{6}+3 t,\frac{9 t^2}{2} - 2 t\right\rangle+\mathbf{r}_0 \end{array} The initial condition \mathbf{r}(0)=\langle 0,0\rangle gives \mathbf{r}_0=\langle 0,0\rangle, so \mathbf{r}(t)=\left\langle \frac{t^3}{6}+3 t,\frac{9 t^2}{2} - 2 t\right\rangle.

= \left\lt \int \sin 9 t dt,\int \sin 4 t dt,\int 9 t dt\right> = \left\lt -\frac{1}{9}\cos 9 t,-\frac{1}{4}\cos 4 t,\frac{9}{2} t^2\right> + \bf c\it Substituting the initial condition we obtain:

We need to reparametrize the curve by making a substitution on t=\phi(s), so that the new parametrization \bf r\it_1(s)=\bf r\it(\phi(s)) satisfies ||\bf r\it_1'(s)||=25 for all s. We find \bf r\it_1' using the Chain Rule:
\bf r\it_1'(s)=\frac{d}{ds}\bf r\it(\phi(s))=\phi'(s)\bf r\it'(\phi(s))
Next, we differentiate \bf r\it(t) and then replace t by \phi(s):
\bf r\it'(t)=\left\lt -5\sin t, 0, 5\cos t\right>
\bf r\it'(\phi(s))=\left\lt -5\sin(\phi(s)), 0, 5\cos(\phi(s))\right>
Now, we get: \bf r\it_1'(s)=\phi'(s)\left\lt -5\sin(\phi(s)), 0, 5\cos(\phi(s))\right>=5\phi'(s)\left\lt -\sin(\phi(s)), 0,\cos(\phi(s))\right>
Hence,
||\bf r\it_1'(s)||=5|\phi'(s)|\sqrt{(-\sin(s))^2+(\cos(s))^2}=5|\phi'(s)|
To satisfy ||\bf r\it_1'(s)||=25 for all s, we choose \phi'(s)=5.
We may take the antiderivative of \phi(s)=5 s and obtain the following parametrization:
\bf r\it_1(s)=\bf r\it(\phi(s))=r(5 s)=\left\lt 1+5\cos (5 s), 4, 3+5\sin (5 s)\right>

static.solution:
\bf r\it_1(s)=\bf r\it(\phi(s)) where t=\phi(s) is the inverse of the arc length function. We compute the arc length function:
s(t)=\int^{t}_{0}||\bf r\it'(u)|| du
Differentiating \bf r\it(t) and computing the norm of \bf r\it'(t) gives:
\bf r\it'(t)=\left\lt e^t\sin t+e^t\cos t, e^t\cos t-e^t\sin t, 3e^{t}\right>
=e^t\left\lt \sin t+\cos t, \cos t-\sin t, 3\right>
||\bf r\it'(t)||=e^t\sqrt{(\sin t+\cos t)^2+(\cos t-\sin t)^2+3^2}=e^t\sqrt{2(\sin^2t+\cos^2t)+9}=\sqrt{11}e^t
Thus,
s(t)=\int^{t}_{0}\sqrt{11}e^udu=\sqrt{11}\left.e^u\right|^{t}_{0}=\sqrt{11}\left(e^t-1\right)
We find the inverse function of s(t) by solving s=\sqrt{11}\left(e^t-1\right) for t. We obtain:
\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}=e^t-1
e^t=1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}
t=\phi(s)=\ln\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}\right)
Thus arc length parametrization for \bf r\it_1(s)=\bf r\it(\phi(s)) is:
\left\lt \left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}\right)\sin\mathopen{}\left(\ln\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}\right)\right), \left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}\right)\cos\mathopen{}\left(\ln\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}\right)\right), 3\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}\right)\right>
=(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}})\left\lt \sin\left(\ln\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}\right)\right), \cos\left(\ln\mathopen{}\left(1+\frac{s}{\sqrt{11}}\right)\right), 3\right>

statement.p: Calculate the length of the path over the given interval. (\sin \theta - \theta \cos \theta, \cos \theta + \theta \sin \theta), \, 0 \le \theta \le 9

static.solution: x = \sin \theta - \theta \cos \theta and y = \cos \theta + \theta \sin \theta. Hence, x' = \cos \theta - \left( \cos \theta - \theta \sin \theta \right) = \theta \sin \theta and y' = - \sin \theta + \sin \theta + \theta \cos \theta = \theta \cos \theta. Using the formula for the arc length we obtain: S = \int ^{9} _0 \sqrt{x'(\theta)^2 + y'(\theta)^2} \, dt = \int ^{9} _0 \sqrt{ \left( \theta \sin \theta \right) ^2 + \left( \theta \cos \theta \right)^2 } \, d \theta = \int ^{9} _0 \sqrt{ \theta^2 \left( \sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta \right) } \, d \theta = \int ^{9} _0 \theta \, d \theta = \frac{\theta^2}{2} \mid ^{9} _0 = \frac{81}{2} = 40.5

statement.p: Find the length of the spiral c(t) = (t \cos t, t \sin t) for 0 \le t \le 2 \pi to three decimal places. Hint: use the formula \int \sqrt{1 + t^2} \, dt = \frac{1}{2} t \sqrt{1 + t^2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln \left( t + \sqrt{1 + t^2} \right) + C

static.solution: S = \int ^{2 \pi} _0 \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} \, dt Differentiating x = t \cos t and y = t \sin t yields x'(t) = \frac{d}{dt} (t \cos t) = \cos t - t \sin t y'(t) = \frac{d}{dt} (t \sin t) = \sin t + t \cos t Thus, \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2} = \sqrt{(\cos t - t \sin t)^2 + (\sin t + t \cos t)^2} = \sqrt{\cos^2 t - 2 t \cos t \sin t + t^2 \sin^2 t + \sin^2 t + 2 t \sin t \cos t + t^2 \cos^2 t} = \sqrt{(\cos^2 t + \sin^2 t)(1 + t^2)} = \sqrt{1 + t^2} We substitute into (1) and use the integral given in the hint to obtain the following arc length: S = \int ^{2 \pi} _0 \sqrt{1 + t^2} \, dt = \frac{1}{2} t \sqrt{1 + t^2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln \left( t + \sqrt{1 + t^2} \right) \mid ^{2 \pi} _0 = \left[\frac{1}{2} \cdot 2 \pi \sqrt{1 + (2 \pi)^2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln \left(2 \pi + \sqrt{1 + (2 \pi)^2} \right)\right] - \left[ 0 + \frac{1}{2} \ln 1 \right] = 1 \pi \sqrt{1 + 4 \pi^2} + \frac{1}{2} \ln \left( 2 \pi + \sqrt{1 + 4 \pi^2} \right) \approx 21.256

This gives: L=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{14}\sqrt{u^2+61}\,du= \left.\frac{1}{4}u\sqrt{u^2+61}+\frac{1}{4}\cdot 61\ln\left(u+\sqrt{u^2+61}\right)\right|_0^{14}=

=\frac{7}{2}\sqrt{257}+\frac{61}{4}\ln\left(14+\sqrt{257}\right) - \frac{61}{4}\ln\sqrt{61}=
\frac{7}{2}\sqrt{257}+\frac{61}{4}\ln\frac{14+\sqrt{257}}{\sqrt{61}} \approx 76.65

statement.p: Sketch a contour diagram of each function. Then, decide whether its contours are predominantly lines, parabolas, ellipses, or hyperbolas.

solution.p: SOLUTION
1. The contours have equation k = x^2+ 2 y^2 , which (for k >0) represent ellipses in the xy- plane.
2. The contours have equation k = y-5 x^2 , which represent parabolas in the xy- plane.
3. The contours have equation k = x^2- 4 y^2 , which represent hyperbolas in the xy- plane.
4. The contours have equation k = -2 x^2. For k \le 0, these equations are equivalent to x = \pm \sqrt{-k/2}, which represent vertical lines in the xy- plane.

solution.p: The revenue function, R, is linear and so we may write it as: R = (p_1)c + (p_2)dwhere p_1 is the price of CDs and p_2 is the price of DVDs, in dollars. From the diagram, we can pick two points, such as c = 200, d=100 on the contour R=2000, and c = 100, d = 300 on the contour R = 3000. These points give the following system of linear equations: 2000 = 200 p_1 + 100 p_2, \mbox{ and } 3000 = 100 p_1 + 300 p_2.Solving gives p_1 = 6 dollars and p_2 = 8 dollars.

Consider the concentration, C, in mg per liter (L), of a drug in the blood as a function of x, the amount, in mg, of the drug given and t, the time in hours since the injection. For 0 \leq x \leq 3 and t \geq 0, we have C = f(x,t) = t e^{-t(4-x)}.
Graph the following two single variable functions on a separate page, being sure that you can explain their significance in terms of drug concentration.
Using your graph in (a), where is f(3,t)
a maximum? t =
a minimum? t =
Using your graph in (b), where is f(x,0.5)
a maximum? x =
a minimum? x =

static.solution:
(a) Holding x fixed at 3 means that we are considering an injection of 3 mg of the drug; letting t vary means we are watching the effect of this dose as time passes. Thus the function f(3,t) describes the concentration of the drug in the blood resulting from a 3 mg injection as a function of time. The figure below shows the graph of f(3,t)=t\,e^{- t}. Notice that the concentration in the blood from this dose is at a maximum at 1 hour after injection, and that the concentration in the blood eventually approaches zero. The initial concentration is 0, so the minimum occurs at t = 0.
(b) Holding t fixed at 0.5 means that we are focusing on the blood 0.5 hours after the injection; letting x vary means we are considering the effect of different doses at that instant. Thus, the function f(x,0.5) gives the concentration of the drug in the blood 0.5 hours after injection as a function of the amount injected. The figure below shows the graph of f(x,0.5)=0.5 e^{-(4-x)}. Notice that f(x,0.5) is an increasing function of x. This makes sense: If we administer more of the drug, the concentration in the bloodstream is higher. In particular, this means that the maximum concentration occurs at the maximum value of x, 3, and the minimum at x = 0.

Match the functions with the graphs of their domains.

static.solution:
\ln\mathopen{}\left(2x+y\right) is the region 2x+y > 0, which is the half-plane with boundary 2x+y = 0.
The domain of 2x+y is the entire plane.
The domain of \sqrt{x^{3}y^{3}} is the region x^{3}y^{3} \geq 0. The domain will include the lines x = 0 and y = 0. The factor x^{3} is positive for all positive x and negative for all negative x. The factor y^{3} is positive for all positive y and negative for all negative y. The product is positive if both factors are positive, or both factors are negative. This occurs in Quadrant I and Quadrant III.
The domain of e^{\frac{1}{2x+y}} is the same as the domain of the exponent. This means that the domain is the same as the domain of \frac{1}{2x+y}, which is the set line 2x+y \neq 0. Thus, the domain is entire plane except for the line 2x+y = 0.

static.solution:
(a) z=2+x^2+y^2 is an upward opening parabaloid with positive z intercept, centered on the z-axis, and so is 3.
(b) z=2-x^2-y^2 is a downward opening parabaloid with positive z intercept, centered on the z-axis, and so is 1.
(c) z=2(x^2 + y^2) is an upward opening parabaloid with zero z intercept, centered on the z-axis, and so is none of these graphs.
(d) z=2 is a plane parallel to the x- and y-axes, with positive z intercept., and so is 2.
(e) z=-2(x^2 + y^2) is a downward opening parabaloid with zero z intercept, centered on the z-axis, and so is 4.
(f) z=-2 is a plane parallel to the x- and y-axes, with negative z intercept., and so is none of these graphs.

?
A

B

static.solution:
(a) The contour lines are much closer together on path A, so path A is steeper.

statement.p: Match the functions with the graphs of their domains.

static.solution:
\ln\mathopen{}\left(y-2x\right) is the region y-2x > 0, which is the half-plane with boundary y-2x = 0.
The domain of y-2x is the entire plane.
The domain of \sqrt{x^{5}y^{5}} is the region x^{5}y^{5} \geq 0. The domain will include the lines x = 0 and y = 0. The factor x^{5} is positive for all positive x and negative for all negative x. The factor y^{5} is positive for all positive y and negative for all negative y. The product is positive if both factors are positive, or both factors are negative. This occurs in Quadrant I and Quadrant III.
The domain of e^{\frac{1}{y-2x}} is the same as the domain of the exponent. This means that the domain is the same as the domain of \frac{1}{y-2x}, which is the set line y-2x \neq 0. Thus, the domain is entire plane except for the line y-2x = 0.

statement.p: Find the limits, if they exist, or type DNE for any which do not exist.
1) Along the x-axis:
2) Along the y-axis:
3) Along the line y=mx :
4) The limit is:
(a) Suppose that we consider (x,y)\to (0,0) along the curve y = 3 x. Find the limit in this case:
(b) Now consider (x,y)\to (0,0) along the curve y = 4 x. Find the limit in this case:
(c) Note that the results from (a) and (b) indicate that f has no limit as (x,y)\to (0,0) (be sure you can explain why!).
To show this more generally, consider (x,y)\to (0,0) along the curve y = m x, for arbitrary m. Find the limit in this case:

p.em: (Be sure that you can explain how this result also indicates that f has no limit as (x,y)\to(0,0).

static.solution:
f does not have a limit as (x,y) approaches (0,0).
(a) If (x,y) tends to (0,0) along the curve y = 3 x, then f(x,y) = f(x,3 x) = \frac{3x^{2}-\left(3x\right)^{2}}{x^{2}+\left(3x\right)^{2}} = \frac{-3}{5}.
Therefore \lim_{x\to0} f(x,3 x) = \frac{-3}{5}.
(b) Similarly, if (x,y) tends to (0,0) along the curve y = 4 x, then f(x,y) = f(x,4 x) = \frac{3x^{2}-\left(4x\right)^{2}}{x^{2}+\left(4x\right)^{2}} = \frac{-13}{17},
and so \lim_{x\to0} f(x,4 x) = \frac{-13}{17}.
Because we have two different values for these limits, we know that the function doesn't have a limit at (0,0). No matter how close we are to the origin, there will be points on f(x,y) that are close to \frac{-3}{5} and points that are close to \frac{-13}{17}, whereas for the limit to exist the function must get close to a single value.
(c) We can see this more generally by considering the limit as (x,y) tends to (0,0) along the curve y = m x. Then f(x,y) = f(x,m x) = \frac{3-m^{2}}{1+m^{2}}, so that \lim_{x\to0} f(x,m x) = \frac{3-m^{2}}{1+m^{2}}, and we see for every different value of m we will get a different limiting value for the function. Thus the function does not have a limit at (0,0).

statement.p: Show that the function f(x,y) = \frac{x^{4}y}{x^{8}+y^{4}}. does not have a limit at (0,0) by examining the following limits.
(a) Find the limit of f as (x,y) \to (0,0) along the line y = x.
(b) Find the limit of f as (x,y)\to(0,0) along the curve y = x^4.

p.em: (Be sure that you are able to explain why the results in (a) and (b) indicate that f does not have a limit at (0,0)!

static.solution:
(a) Let us suppose that (x,y) approaches (0,0) along the line y=x. Then f(x,y) = f(x,x) = \frac{x^5}{x^{8} + x^4} = \frac{x}{x^4+1}. Therefore \lim_{^{(x,y)\to(0,0)}_{y=x}} f(x,y) = \lim_{x\to0} \frac{x}{x^4+1} = 0.
(b) On the other hand, if (x,y) approaches (0,0) along the curve y=x^4 we have f(x,y)=f(x,x^4) = \frac{x^{8}}{x^{8} + x^{16}} = 1 and so \lim_{^{(x,y)\to(0,0)}_{y=x^4}} f(x,y) = \lim_{x\to0}f(x,x^4) = 1.
Thus no matter how close they are to the origin, there will be points (x,y) such that f(x,y) is close to 0 and points (x,y) such that f(x,y) is close to 1. So the limit \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} f(x,y) does not exist.

Find the limit of the function f(x,y) = \frac{\sin(4\mathopen{}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right))}{4\mathopen{}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)} as (x,y) \to (0,0). Assume that polynomials, exponentials, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions are continuous. [Hint: \lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\sin t}{t}=1.]

p.em: (Enter DNE if the limit does not exist.)

static.solution: \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)} f(x,y) = \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}\frac{\sin(4\mathopen{}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right))}{4\mathopen{}\left(x^{2}+y^{2}\right)}. As r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} is the distance from (x,y) to (0,0) we have that (x,y) \to (0,0) is equivalent to r \to 0. Hence the limit becomes: \lim_{(x,y)\to(0,0)}f(x,y) = \lim _{r\to0}\frac{\sin 4r^{2}}{4r^{2}} = 1.

statement.p: For the function f(x,y) below, determine whether there is a value for c making the function continuous everywhere. If so, find it. f(x,y) = \begin{cases} c + y \amp x \le 4, \\ 2 - y \amp x > 4 \end{cases}

p.em: (If there is no value of c that works, enter none, and be sure that you can explain why there is no such value.)

static.solution:
f is continuous at all points (x,y) with x \neq 4. So let's analyze the continuity of f at the point (4,a). We have \lim_{^{(x,y)\to(4,a)}_{x\lt 4}} f(x,y) = \lim_{y \to a} (c+y) = c+a and \lim_{^{(x,y)\to(4,a)}_{x>4}} f(x,y) = \lim_{y \to a} (2-y) = 2-a.
So we need to see if we can find one value for c such that c+a=5-a for all a. This would require that c=5-2a, but then c would depend on a, which is exactly what we don't want. Therefore, we cannot make the function continuous everywhere.
Graphically we can see this by thinking about what the function looks like: for x \le 4, it is a plane with positive y-slope, passing through the line y=0, z=c. For x > 4, it is a plane with negative y-slope, pssing through the line y=0, z = y_0 = 2. This is shown in the figure below.

f(x,y) = x^{3}+y^{4}+4 gets closer and closer to 4 as (x,y) gets closer to the origin. To make f continuous at the origin, we need to have f(0,0) = 4. Thus c=4 will make the function continuous at the origin.

static.solution:
(a)-(d) We have f(x,0)=0 for all x and f(0,y)=0 for all y, and obviously \lim\limits_{x\to0} f(x,0) = 0 = \lim\limits_{y\to0} f(0,y), so these are both continuous (constant) functions of one variable.
(e) Along y = x, we have f(x,y) = f(x,x) = 4. Because this is a constant value, this is a contour of f. Similarly, along any ray y = m x, we have f(x,y) = f(x, mx) = \frac{8 m}{m^2 + 1}, which is also a constant, and we therefore have that all such rays are contours of the function f.
(f) Finally, notice that because we know f(x,y) = 4 along the line y = x, and f(x,0) = 0, we can see that no matter how close we are to the origin, we can find points (x,y) where the value f(x,y) is 4 and points (x,y) where the value f(x,y) is 0. So the limit \lim\limits_{(x,y)\to (0,0)}f(x,y) does not exist. Thus, f is not continuous at (0,0), even though the one-variable functions f(x,0) and f(0,y) are continuous at (0,0).

statement.p: An experiment to measure the toxicity of formaldehyde yielded the data in the table below. The values show the percent, P=f(t,c), of rats surviving an exposure to formaldehyde at a concentration of c (in parts per million, ppm) after t months.
(a) Estimate f_t(20,2):
(b) Estimate f_c(20,2):

p.em: (Be sure that you can give the practical meaning of these two values in terms of formaldehyde toxicity.)

static.solution:
f(20,2) = 97.
(a) Thus, to estimate f_t(20,2), we can take f_t(20,2) \approx \frac{f(20+2,2) - f(20-2,2)}{4} = \frac{95 - 98}{4} = -0.75. Alternately, we could take either of the two one-sided difference quotients, f_t(20,2) \approx \frac{f(20+2,2) - f(20,2)}{2} = -1 or f_t(20,2) \approx \frac{f(20,2) - f(20-2,2)}{2} = -0.5. In each case, the units of f_t are percent per month. This says 20 months after rats are exposed to a formaldehyde concentration of 2 ppm, the percent of rats surviving is decreasing at a rate of about -0.75 per month. In other words, during the 20 month, around an additional -0.75 percent of the rats will die.
(b) Proceeding similarly to find f_c(20,2), we have f_c(20,2) \approx \frac{f(20,2+2) - f(20,2-2)}{4} = \frac{90 - 99}{4} = -1.5, or, with one-sided difference quotients, f_c(20,2) \approx \frac{f(20,2+2) - f(20,2)}{2} = -1.75 or f_c(20,2) \approx \frac{f(20,2) - f(20,2-2)}{2} = -1. These indicate that if the original concentration increases from 2 by 1 ppm, the percent surviving after 20 months decreases by about 1.5.

static.solution:
(a) The quantity H_T(10,0.2) is approximated by an difference quotient. If we take \Delta T = 10, we get the approximation H_T(10,0.2) \approx { H(20, 0.2) - H(10, 0.2)\over 10} \approx {190 - 240\over 10} = -5.
(Note that you may get a different answer if you read different values from the graph.) The geometric meaning of the partial derivative H_T(10,0.2) that we just approximated is the slope of the curve shown in the figure in the text corresponding to w = 0.2 at the point where T= 10.
In practical terms, we have found that for fog at 10^\circ C containing 0.1 g water per m{}^3 of fog, a 1^\circ C increase in temperature will reduce the heat requirement for dissipating the fog by about 1~calories per cubic meter of fog.
(b) We can approximate values of H(T,w) from the figure, giving the table below:
w = 0.1 0.2 0.3 0.4
T = 10 120 240 330 450
T = 20 100 190 260 350
T = 30 80 160 220 300
T = 40 70 130 200 280
This lets us approximate, using a difference quotient, each of the derivatives indicated. For H_T(20,0.2), we have H_T(20,0.2) \approx \frac{(160 - 190)}{10} = -3. (We could, of course, use a left or central difference instead.) Similarly, we have: H_T(30,0.2) \approx -3, H_T(20,w2) \approx -4, H_T(30,0.3) \approx -2.
(c) Using our table of values, we can similarly calculate the partial derivatives with respect to w. For H_w(20,0.2), we have H_w(20,0.2) \approx \frac{(260 - 190)}{0.1} = 700. (We could, of course, use a left or central difference instead.) Similarly, we have: H_w(30,0.2) \approx 600, H_w(20,w2) \approx 900, H_w(30,0.3) \approx 800.

The following questions refer to the table shown below, giving the temperature adjusted for wind-chill, C, in {}^\circ F, as a function f(w,T) of the wind speed, w, in mph, and the temperature, T, in {}^\circ F. The temperature adjusted for wind-chill tells you how cold it feels, as a result of the combination of wind and temperature.
(a) Estimate f_w(5, 15):

p.em: Be sure you can state in practical terms what your answer means.

statement.p: (b) Estimate f_T(5, 35):

p.em: Be sure you can state in practical terms what your answer means.

static.solution:
(a) For f_w(5, 15) we know f_w(w_0, t_0) \approx \frac{f(w_0 + h,t_0) - f(w_0,t_0)}{h}.
Thus, we have f_w(5, 15) \approx \frac{(3 - 7)}{5} = -0.8.
This means that when the wind speed is 5 mph and the true temperature is 15 {}^\circ F, as the wind speed increases from 5 mph by 1 mph we feel an approximately -0.8^\circ F drop in temperature. This rate is negative because the temperature you feel drops as the wind speed increases.
(b) For f_t(5, 35) we know f_t(w_0, t_0) \approx \frac{f(w_0,t_0 + h) - f(w_0,t_0)}{h}.
Thus, we have f_t(5, 35) \approx \frac{(31 - 25)}{5} = 1.2.
This means that when the wind speed is 5 mph and the true temperature is 35 {}^\circ F, the apparent temperature increases by approximately 1.2^\circ F for an increase of 1^\circ F in the true temperature. This rate is positive because the temperature you feel increases as the true temperature increases.

A one-meter long bar is heated unevenly, with temperature in {}^\circC at a distance x meters from one end at time t given by H(x,t) = 100e^{-0.15t}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right) 0\le x\le 1. On a sheet of paper, sketch a graph of H against x for t=0 and t=1. Think about why your graphs make sense.
(a) Calculate each of:

p.em: (Be sure that you can say in words what the practical interpretation (in terms of temperature) of these two partial derivatives is, and why each has the sign that it does.)

statement.p: (b) Calculate:
H_t(x,t) = .

p.em: (Again, be sure that you understand why it has the sign that it does, and what its interpretation in terms of temperature is.)

static.solution:
t=0 and t=1 into the formula for H gives: H(x,0) = 100e^{0}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right), and H(x,1) = 100e^{-0.15}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right). The graphs of these are shown below (with H(x,0) in red and H(x,1) in blue).
Note that this makes sense: it says that the bar starts with a varying temperature distribution, and that as time goes on the temperature decays at all points on the bar towards a temperature of zero.
(a) To calculate H_x(x,t), we hold t constant and differentiate with respect to x: H_x(x,t) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}H(x,t) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x} 100e^{-0.15t}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right) = 100e^{-0.15t}\pi \cos\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right). Thus H_x(0.2,t) = 100\pi e^{-0.15 t}\cos(0.2 \pi) = 100e^{-0.15t}\pi \cos\mathopen{}\left(\pi \cdot 0.2\right)\quad {}^\circ\hbox{C/meter}, and H_x(0.8,t) = 100\pi e^{-0.15 t}\cos(0.8 \pi) = 100e^{-0.15t}\pi \cos\mathopen{}\left(\pi \cdot 0.8\right)\quad {}^\circ\hbox{C/meter}. The practical interpretation of these partial derivatives is the rate of change in temperature at x=0.2 and x=0.8 as we increase the distance from the end x=0. Notice that e^{-0.15 t} is positive for all t. Given the formula for H(x,t), we see that the closer the position to the center of the rod, the hotter the temperature. The partial derivative H_x(0.2,t) has a positive sign because, at x=0.2 as we increase x, we get closer to the center of the rod, which is hottest. The partial derivative H_x(0.8,t) has a negative sign because, at x=0.8, as we increase x, we get further away from the center of the rod which is hottest.
(b) To calculate H_t(x,t), we hold x constant and differentiate with respect to t: \frac{\partial H}{\partial t}=\frac{\partial}{\partial t}(100e^{-0.15t}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right)) = -15e^{-0.15t}\sin\mathopen{}\left(\pi x\right)\quad {}^\circ\hbox{C/second}. For all t, and for 0\lt x\lt 1 (that is, for all t and all x inside the rod), the partial derivative H_t(x,t) is negative. In terms of heat, H_t(x,t) represents the rate at which the temperature of the rod is changing as time passes at position x and time t. Thus, the temperature inside the rod is always decreasing.

statement.p: Suppose that z is a linear function of x and y with slope 1 in the x direction and slope -2 in the y direction.
(a) A change of 0.1 in x and -0.4 in y produces what change in z?
change in z =
(b) If z=2 when x=3 and y=3, what is the value of z when x=3.2 and y=3?

static.solution:
(a) Since z is a linear function of x and y with slope 1 in the x direction, and slope -2 in the y direction, we have: z = 1 x - 2 y + c. We can write an equation for changes in z in terms of changes in x and y: \Delta z = (1 (x + \Delta x) - 2(y + \Delta y) + c) - (1 x - 2 y + c) = 1 \Delta x - 2 \Delta y. Since \Delta x = 0.1 and \Delta y = -0.4, we have \Delta z = 1 (0.1) - 2(-0.4) = 0.9. So a 0.1 change in x and a -0.4 change in y produces a 0.9 change in z.
(b) As we know that z=2 when x=3 and y=3, the value of z when x=3.2 and y=3 will be z = 2 + \Delta z = 2 + 1\Delta x - 2\Delta y. where \Delta z is the change in z when x changes from 3 to 3.2 and y changes from 3 to 3. We have \Delta x = 3.2 - 3 = 0.2 and \Delta y = 3 - 3 = 5.55111512312578e-17. Therefore, when x=3.2 and y=3, we have z = 2 + 1 \cdot(0.2) - 2\cdot(5.55111512312578e-17) = 2.2.

statement.p: The table below gives the number of calories burned per minute for someone roller-blading, as a function of the person's weight in pounds and speed in miles per hour [from the August 28,1994, issue of Parade Magazine].
(a) Suppose that a 180 lb person and a 200 person both go 10 miles, the first at 11 mph and the second at 10 mph.
How many calories does the 180 lb person burn?
How many calories does the 200 lb person burn?
(b) We might also be interested in the number of calories each person burns per pound of their weight.
How many calories per pound does the 180 lb person burn?
How many calories per pound does the 200 lb person burn?

static.solution:
(a) The time in minutes to go 10 miles at a speed of s mph is (10/s)(60)= 600/s. Thus the 180 lb person going 11 mph uses (11.7)(600/11) = 638.182 calories, and the 200 lb person going 10 mph uses (11.1)(600/10) = 666 calories.
(b) The 180 lb person burns 638.182/180 = 3.54546 calories per pound for the trip, while the 200 lb person burns 666/200 = 3.33 calories per pound for the trip.

statement.p: A fluid moves through a tube of length 1 meter and radius r = 0.004 \pm 0.0002 meters under a pressure p = 5\cdot 10^5 \pm 1250 pascals, at a rate v= 0.875 \cdot 10^{-9} \hbox{m}^3 per unit time. Use differentials to estimate the maximum error in the viscosity \eta given by \eta = \frac{ \pi}{8} \frac{p r^4}{v}.
maximum error \approx

static.solution:
\eta is approximated by d\eta, where d\eta = \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} dr + \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial p} dp.
We need to find \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r}=\frac{ \pi}{8} \frac{p 4 r^3}{v } and \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial p}=\frac{ \pi}{8} \frac{ r^4}{v}. For r = 0.004, v = 0.875\cdot 10^{-9} and p=5\cdot 10^5 we get \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r}(0.004,5\cdot 10^5) = \frac{ \pi}{8} \frac{(5\cdot 10^5)(4\, (0.004)^3)}{0.875\cdot 10^{-9}} = 5.74463\times 10^{7}, and similarly \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial p}(0.004, 5\cdot 10^5) = 0.114893, so that d\eta = \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial r} d r + \frac{\partial \eta}{\partial p} dp. is largest when we take all positive values to give d\eta = (5.74463\times 10^{7})(0.0002) + (0.114893)(1250) = 11632.9.
This seems quite large, but \eta(0.004,5\cdot 10^5) = 57446.3, so the maximum error represents about 20 % of any value computed by the given formula. Notice also the relative error in r is \pm 5 %, which means that the relative error in r^4 is \pm 10 %.

statement.p: The monthly payment for a home loan is given by a function f(P,r,N) where P is the principal (the initial size of the loan), r the interest rate, and N the length of the loan in months. statement.p: Find the linear approximation to f(x,y,z)=\frac{xy}{z} at the point (2,1,-2):

(2,1,-2):

statement.p: Find a vector parametric equation for the line perpendicular to the surface z = 4 x^2 + 3 y^2 at the point (3,3,63).

static.solution: f(x,y,z) = 4 x^2 + 3 y^2 - z. Then the surface z = 4 x^2 + 3 y^2 is a level surface of f at the value 0. The gradient of f is perpendicular to the level surface. \nabla f(3,3,63) = (8 x\,\vec i + 6 y\,\vec j - \vec k)\bigg|_{(3,3,63)} = 24\,\mathit{\vec i}+18\,\mathit{\vec j}-\,\mathit{\vec k}. So a possible parameterization is \vec r(t) = \left(3+24t\right)\,\mathit{\vec i}+\left(3+18t\right)\,\mathit{\vec j}+\left(63-t\right)\,\mathit{\vec k}.

statement.p: A differentiable function f(x,y) has the property that f(4,1)=3 and f_x(4,1)=2 and f_y(4,1)=3. Find the equation of the tangent plane at the point on the surface z=f(x,y) where x=4, y=1.

static.solution: (4,1,3) lies on the surface. The surface is the level surface of the function F(x,y,z) = f(x,y) - z = 0 . The normal to the surface at the point (4,1,3) is \nabla F(4,1,3) = f_x(4,1)\vec i + f_y(4,1)\vec j - \vec k= 2 \vec i + 3 \vec j - \vec k. Thus the equation of the tangent plane is 2 x + 3 y - z = 2 (4) + 3 (1) - 3 or z = 3+2\mathopen{}\left(x-4\right)+3\mathopen{}\left(y-1\right).

statement.p: Corn production, C, is a function of rainfall, R (in inches), and temperature, T (in degrees C). The first figure below shows how rainfall is predicted to vary with time because of global warming; the second, how temperature is predicted to vary with time because of global warming.
Graph of rainfall, R vs. time, t
Graph of temperature, T vs. time, t
Suppose that we know that (currently) \Delta C \approx 2.9 \Delta R - 5.3 \Delta T
Use this to estimate the change in corn production between the year 2020 and the year 2021.
Change =
Hence, estimate dC/dt when t=2020.

static.solution:
R=15 inches and T=25^\circC, a change, \Delta R, in rainfall and a change, \Delta T, in temperature produces a change, \Delta C, in corn production given by \Delta C \approx 2.9 \Delta R - 5.3 \Delta T. Now both R and T are functions of time t (in years), and we want to find the effect of a small change in time, \Delta t, on R and T. The first figure shows that the slope of the graph for R versus t is about -0.7/10 = -0.07 in/year when t=2020. Similarly, the second shows the slope of the graph of T versus t is about 0.8/10 = 0.08^\circ C/year when t=2020. Thus, around the year 2020, \Delta R \approx -0.07 \Delta t \quad \mbox{ and} \quad \Delta T \approx 0.08 \Delta t.
Substituting these into the equation for \Delta C, we get \Delta C \approx (2.9)(-0.07) \Delta t - (5.3)(0.08) \Delta t \approx -0.627 \Delta t.
Thus in one year corn production will decline by about 0.627 in.
When t=2020 \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta t}\approx -0.627, so \frac{dC}{dt}\approx -0.627.

statement.p: Air pressure decreases at a rate of 1.25 pascals per kilometer in the eastward direction. In addition, the air pressure is decreasing at a constant rate with respect to time everywhere. A ship sailing eastward at 10 km/hour past an island takes barometer readings and records a pressure drop of 50 pascals in 2 hours. Estimate the time rate of change of air pressure on the island. (A pascal is a unit of air pressure.)
Time rate of change of air pressure =
(include )

static.solution:
p(x,t) be the air pressure in pascals at x km east of the island at time t hours after the ship passes the island. We want to compute \partial p/\partial t.
Let S(t) be the air pressure on the ship at time t, so that S(t)=p(10 t, t). By the chain rule we have {dS\over dt} = {\partial p\over \partial x}{dx\over dt} + {\partial p\over \partial t}{dt\over dt} = {\partial p\over \partial x}{dx\over dt} + {\partial p\over \partial t}. Since dS/dt \approx (-50 \hbox{ pascal})/(2 \hbox{ hour}) = -25 \mbox{ pascal}/\mbox{hour}, and \partial p/ \partial x = -1.25\hbox{ pascal/km}, and dx / dt = 10 \hbox{ km/hour}, solving for \partial p / \partial t, we have {\partial p \over \partial t} = -25 \hbox{ pascal/hour} + (1.25 \hbox{ pascal/km}) (10 \hbox{ km/hour} ) = -12.5\ {\textstyle\frac{\rm\mathstrut Pa}{\rm\mathstrut hr}}

statement.p: Use the Chain Rule to evaluate the partial derivative \frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta} at the point (r,\theta)=(2\sqrt 2,\frac{\pi}4)
where g(x,y) = \frac{1}{6 x+7 y^2}, x=r\sin\theta, y=r\cos\theta.

static.solution:
g( x,y )=\frac{1}{6 x+7 {y}^2}: \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}=-\frac{6}{{(6 x+7 {y}^2)}^2},\quad \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}=-\frac{14 y}{{(6 x+7 {y}^2)}^2} By the Chain Rule we have \begin{array}{rcl} \frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta }\amp =\amp \frac{\partial g}{\partial x} \frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta }+\frac{\partial g}{\partial y} \frac{\partial y}{\partial \theta }\\ \amp =\amp -\frac{6}{{(6 x+7 {y}^2)}^2} \frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta }-\frac{14 y}{{(6 x+7 {y}^2)}^2} \frac{\partial y}{\partial \theta }\\ \amp =\amp -\frac{1}{{(6 x+7 {y}^2)}^2}\left(6\frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta }+14 y \frac{\partial y}{\partial \theta }\right) \end{array} We find the partial derivatives \frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta }, \frac{\partial y}{\partial \theta }: \frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta }=r \cos \theta ,\quad \frac{\partial y}{\partial \theta }=-r \sin \theta Hence, \frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta }=-\frac{r}{{(6 x+7 {y}^2)}^2} (6\cos\theta -14 y \sin \theta ) \quad \mathbf{(1)} At the point ( r,\theta )=\bigl(2\sqrt{2},\frac{\pi }{4}\bigr), we have x=2\sqrt{2} \sin \frac{\pi }{4}=2 and y=2\sqrt{2} \cos \frac{\pi }{4}=2.
Substituting ( r,\theta )=\bigl(2\sqrt{2},\frac{\pi }{4}\bigr) and ( x,y )=( 2,2 ) in \mathbf{(1)} gives the following derivative: \begin{array}{rcl} \left.\frac{\partial g}{\partial \theta }\right|_{( r,\theta)=\left(2\sqrt{2},\frac{\pi}{4}\right)} \amp =\amp \frac{-2\sqrt{2}}{{(12+7\cdot {2}^2)}^2} \left(6\cos \frac{\pi }{4}-28 \sin \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\\ \amp =\amp \frac{-\sqrt{2}}{800}\left(\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{28}{\sqrt{2}}\right)=\frac{11}{400}. \end{array}

statement.p: At a certain point on a heated metal plate, the greatest rate of temperature increase, 2 degrees Celsius per meter, is toward the northeast. If an object at this point moves directly north, at what rate is the temperature increasing?
degrees Celsius per meter

solution.p: SOLUTION
Let T be the temperature function and P the point. The value of the greatest rate of increase is the magnitude of the gradient. Thus \left| \nabla T (P) \right| = 2.
The gradient points in the northeast direction, so \nabla T (P) = \left \langle 2 \cos (45^o) , 2 \sin (45^o) \right \rangle = \left \langle \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}, \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \right \rangle.

A unit vector in the north direction is \mathbf{u} = \langle 0, 1 \rangle, so the rate of change of increase of the temperature in that direction is D_{\mathbf u} T(P) = \nabla T (P) \cdot \mathbf{u} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}

static.solution:
(a) The unit vector \mathbf{u} in the same direction as \mathbf{v} is \mathbf{u} = \frac{1}{\Vert \mathbf{v}\Vert} \mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{8}} \mathbf{v} = \langle \frac{2}{\sqrt{8}}, \frac{-2}{\sqrt{8}} \rangle \approx \left\lt 0.707107,-0.707107\right>.
The vector \mathbf{w} of length 0.1 in the direction of \mathbf{v} is \vec w = 0.1\vec u = \left\lt 0.0707107,-0.0707107\right> The displacement vector from P to Q is \mathbf{w}. Hence Q = (7,4) + (0.0707107, -0.0707107) = (7.07071, 3.92929).
(b) Since the distance from P to Q is 0.1, the directional derivative of f at P in the direction of Q is approximately f_{u} \approx \frac{f(Q)-f(P)}{0.1} = \frac{3.31662 - 3.31662}{0.1} = 0.
(c) We have f_x = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1y}}\quad\mbox{and}\quad f_y = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+1y}}, so \nabla f(7,4) = \left\lt 0.150756,0.150756\right>.
The directional derivative at P=(7, 4) in the direction of \mathbf{u} is f_u(7,4) = \nabla f(7,4)\cdot \mathbf{u} = 0.

p.em: (Think about how your answers to these questions are related to the level curves through that point!)

static.solution:
(a) To find the level curves, we let T be a constant. T = 100 - x^2 - y^2,\mbox{ so } x^2+y^2 = 100-T, which is an equation for a circle of radius \sqrt{100-T} centered at the origin.
At T=100^{\circ}, we have a circle of radius 0 (a point).
At T=75^{\circ}, we have a circle of radius 5.
At T=50^{\circ}, we have a circle of radius 5\sqrt{2}.
At T=25^{\circ}, we have a circle of radius 5\sqrt{3}.
At T=0^{\circ}, we have a circle of radius 10.
No matter where we put the bug, it should go straight toward the origin---the hottest point on the xy-plane. Its direction of motion is perpendicular to the tangent lines of the level curves. Thus,
at (-7.5, 7.5) the bug should go SE,
at (7.5, 0) the bug should go W,
and at (0, -7.5) the bug should go N.

For both parts of this problem, be sure you can explain what the practical meanings of the partial derivatives are.

static.solution:
\partial P /\partial t: The unit is dollars per month (dollars/month). This is the rate at which payments change as the number of months it takes to pay off the loan changes. The sign is negative because payments decrease as the pay-off time increases. Thus \partial P /\partial t = -15 dollars/month.
\partial P /\partial r: The unit is dollars per percentage point (dollars/percent). This is the rate at which payments change as the interest rate changes. The sign is positive because payments increase as the interest rate increases. Thus \partial P /\partial r = 20 dollars/percent.

statement.p: Find a function f(x,y,z) whose level surface f=8 is the graph of the function g(x,y)= 6x+7y.

static.solution:
g(x,y)=6x+7y is the set of all points (x,y,z) satisfying z=6x+7y, or 6x+7y - z = 0. This is a level surface, but we want the surface equal to the constant value 8, not 0, so we can add 8 to both sides to get 6x+7y - z + 8 = 8. Thus, f(x,y,z) = 6x+7y-z+8 has level surface f=8 identical to the graph of g(x,y)= 6x+7y.
Of course, we could also say that the graph of g(x,y) is equivalent to z - 6x+7y = 0, so that f = z-6x-7y+8.

statement.p: Describe in words the level surfaces of g(x,y,z) = e^{-\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\right)}. Think what the intersections of these surfaces with the three coordinate planes look like.
(a) In symbolic form, these level surfaces are given by e^{-\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\right)} = c where c is a constant. For what values of c are level surfaces defined?

p.em: (Give your answer as an interval or list of intervals; for example, if c is less than 1 or greater than or equal to 2, enter (-inf,1),[2,inf).)

statement.p: (b) Pick a level surface that intersects the xz-plane. What is your value of c?
Write the equation for the intersection, as an expression set equal to a constant:
(c) Pick a level surface that intersects the yz-plane. What is your value of c (which might be different from that you used in (a)?
Write the equation for the intersection, as an expression set equal to a constant:
(d) Pick a level surface that intersects the xy-plane. What is your value of c?
Write the equation for the intersection, as an expression set equal to a constant:

static.solution:
(a) The level surfaces are the graphs of g(x,y,z) = e^{-\left(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}\right)} = c for constant values of c such that 0 \lt c \lt \infty.
Then x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2} = -\ln c, which is the graph of a sphere since -\ln c \ge 0 (or a point if c=1).
(b) In the xz-plane, y=0, so the intersections of the level surfaces with the plane are circles, x^{2}+z^{2} = -\ln(c). Thus we must have c \le e^{-0}, for example, c = 1, for which the intersection of the level curve with the xz-plane is x^{2}+z^{2} = 1.
(c) Similarly, in the yz-plane, x=0, so the intersections of the level surfaces with the plane are circles, y^{2}+z^{2} = -\ln(c). Thus we must have c \le 1, for example, c = e^{-1}, for which the intersection of the level curve with the xz-plane is y^{2}+z^{2} = 1.
(d) Finally, in the xz-plane, z=0, so the intersections of the level surfaces with the plane are circles, x^{2}+y^{2} = -\ln(c). Thus we must have c \le 1, for example, c = e^{-1}, for which the intersection of the level curve with the xz-plane is x^{2}+y^{2} = 1.

Suppose f(x, y) = xy - ax - by.
(A) How many local minimum points does f have in \mathbf{R}^{2}? (The answer is an integer).

(C) How many saddle points does f have in \mathbf{R}^{2}?
Let f(x,y) = 2/x + 3/y + 4 x + 5 y in the region R where x, y > 0.
Explain why f must have a global minimum at some point in R (note that R is unbounded---how does this influence your explanation?). Then find the global minimum.
minimum =

static.solution:
f is continuous in the region R, but R is not closed and bounded so a special analysis is required.
Notice that f(x,y) tends to \infty as (x,y) tends farther and farther from the origin or tends toward any point on the x or y axis. This suggests that a minimum for f, if it exists, can not be too far from the origin or too close to the axes. For example, if x > 10 then f(x,y) > 4 x > 40, and if y > 10 then f(x,y) > 5 y > 50. If 0\lt x\lt 0.1 then f(x,y) > 2/x > 20, and if 0\lt y\lt 0.1 then f(x,y) > 3/y > 30.
Since f(1,1)=14, a global minimum for f if it exists must be in the smaller region R^\prime: 0.1 \le x \le 10, 0.1 \le y \le 10. The region R^\prime is closed and bounded and so have a minimum value at some point in R^\prime, and since that value is at most 14, it is also a global minimum for all of R.
Since the region R has no boundary, the minimum value must occur at a critical point of f. At a critical point we have f_x = -{2\over x^2} + 4 = 0 = f_y = -{3\over y^2} + 5 = 0. The only critical point is (\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}, \sqrt{\frac{3}{5}}), at which f achieves the minimum value f(\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}},\sqrt{\frac{3}{5}}) = 2\sqrt{8} + 2\sqrt{15}

A closed rectangular box has volume 30\,\mbox{cm}^3. What are the lengths of the edges giving the minimum surface area?

p.em: (Give the three lengths as a comma separated list.)

static.solution:
x,y, z cm. Then the volume is given by V = xyz = 30.
The surface area S is given by S = 2xy+2xz+2yz. Substituting z = 30/(xy) gives S = 2xy +\frac{60}{y} + \frac{60}{x}. At a critical point, \frac{\partial S}{\partial x} = 2y - \frac{60}{x^2} = 0, and \frac{\partial S}{\partial y} = 2x - \frac{60}{y^2} = 0.
The symmetry of the equations (or by dividing the equations) tells us that x=y and so that 2x - \frac{60}{x^2} = 0, so that x^3 = 30, \quad\mbox{and so}\quad x = 30^{1/3}\mbox{ cm}. Thus the only critical point is x = y = (30)^{1/3} cm, and z = 30/\left ( (30)^{1/3} \cdot (30)^{1/3} \right ) = (30)^{1/3} cm. At the critical point S_{xx} S_{yy}-(S_{xy})^2= \frac{120}{x^3}\cdot\frac{120}{y^3}-2^2= \frac{(120)^2}{x^{3}y^{3}}-4. Since D>0 and S_{xx}>0 at this critical point, the critical point x = y = z = (30)^{1/3} is a local minimum. Since S\rightarrow\infty as x,y\rightarrow\infty, the local minimum is a global minimum.

static.solution:

At a critical point \frac{\partial S}{\partial x} = y - \frac{68}{x^2} = 0, and \frac{\partial S}{\partial y} = x - \frac{68}{y^2} = 0.
The symmetry of the equations tells us that x=y, so x - \frac{68}{x^2} = 0, \quad\mbox{and}\quad x^3 = 68, so that x = (68)^{1/3} cm.
Thus the only critical point is x=y=(68)^{1/3} cm and z = 34/((68)^{1/3}\cdot (68)^{1/3}) = (17/2)^{1/3} cm.
At the critical point D = S_{xx}S_{yy}-(S_{xy})^2 =\frac{136}{x^3} \cdot \frac{136}{y^3}-1^2= \frac{136^2}{x^3y^3}-1. Since D>0 and S_{xx}>0 at this critical point, the critical point x = y = (68)^{1/3}, z = (17/2)^{1/3} is a local minimum. Since S\rightarrow\infty as x,y\rightarrow\infty, the local minimum is a global minimum.

statement.p: What is the shortest distance from the surface x y + 9 x + z^2 = 73 to the origin?
distance =

static.solution:
(x,y,z) to the origin: S=x^2+y^2+z^2. Since z^2 = 73 - x y - 9 x, we have S = x^2 + y^2 + 73 - x y - 9 x. At a critical point \frac{\partial S}{\partial x} = 2 x - y - 9 = 0, and \frac{\partial S}{\partial y} = 2 y - x = 0, so x = 2 y, and 2(2 y) - y - 9 = 0 giving y=3, so x=6 and z^2 = 73 - (6)(3) - 9 (6), so z=\pm 1. We have D= S_{xx}S_{yy}-(S_{xy})^2 =2\cdot2 - (-1)^2 = 4 - 1 > 0, so, since D>0 and S_{xx}>0, the critical points are local minima. Since S\rightarrow\infty as x,y\rightarrow\pm\infty, the local minima are global minima.
If x=6, y=3, z=\pm 1, we have S = 6^2 + 3^2 + 1^2 = 46, so the shortest distance to the origin is \sqrt{46}.

Design a rectangular milk carton box of width w, length l, and height h which holds 522 \text{ cm}^3 of milk. The sides of the box cost 2 \ \text{cents/cm}^2 and the top and bottom cost 3\ \text{cents/cm}^2. Find the dimensions of the box that minimize the total cost of materials used.
width = , length = , height =
(Include units in your answers.) ( )

solution.p: The total cost of the four sides is (2hl+2wh)(2) cents. The cost of top and bottom is (2wl)(3) cents. Thus the total cost C (in cents) of the box is C = (2)(2)(h)(l+w) + (2)(3) wl. The volume in \text{cm}^3 is wlh = 522, so w,l,h are nonzero and we may divide and obtain l = \frac{522}{wh}. Plug this into the equation for C to obtain \begin{aligned} C \amp = (2)(2)h\left(\frac{522}{wh} + w\right) + (2)(3)(w)\frac{(522)}{wh}\\ \amp =\frac{(2)(2)(522)}{w} + (2)(2)hw + \frac{(2)(3)(522)}{h} \end{aligned} as a function of h and w. To minimize C, find the critical points of C by solving 0=C_h = (2)(2) w - \frac{(2)(3)(522)}{h^2} hence 2 wh^2 = (3)(522), and 0=C_w = \frac{(-2)(2)(522)}{w^2}+(2)(2)h so w^2h = 522. The quotient of these two results is \frac{2 wh^2}{w^2h} = \frac{(3)(522)}{522} so 2 h/w = 3 and h = \frac{3}{2} w .

Plug that into the equation w^2h = 522 to obtain 3 w^3 / 2 = 522 so w^3 = \frac{(2)(522)}{3}, h^3 = \left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^3 w^3 = \frac{(3^2)(522)}{2^2} and, l^3 = \frac{521}{w^3 h^3} = \frac{(2)(522)}{3} = w^3. Hence w = l = \left(\frac{(2)(522)}{3}\right)^{1/3}\approx {7.03385}, and h = \frac{3}{2} w \approx {10.5508}, centimeters.

Next we check that these dimensions minimize the cost C. At the critical point we find that C_{hh} = \frac{(6)(3)(522)}{h^3} = \frac{(6)(2^2)}{3} C_{ww} = \frac{(6)(2)(522)}{w^3} = (6)(3) C_{hw} = (2)(2)
so

D=C_{hh}C_{ww}-C^2_{hw} = (6^2)(2^2)-(2^2)(2^2) > 0. So, at the critical point, D > 0 and C_{hh} > 0 hence C has a local minimum. Since C has no other critical points, and C increases without bound as (w,h)\to (0,0) and as (w,h)\to(\infty,\infty), this local minimum must be a global minimum.
Therefore, the dimensions of the box that minimize the cost are w=l \approx {7.03385}\ cm and h \approx {10.5508}\ cm.

f_x = 0 and f_y = 0 for x and y. Solving f_x = 3x^2 - 18 x = 0, we have x = 0 or x = 6. Then f_y = 3y^2 - 12 = 0, so that y = \pm 2. There are four critical points: (0,2), (0,-2), (6,2), and (6,-2).
Then we have D =(f_{xx})(f_{yy}) - (f_{xy})^2 = (6x-18)(6y) - (0)^2 = (6x-18)(6y). At the point (0,2), we have D \lt 0, so f has saddle point.
At the point (0,-2), we have D > 0 and f_{xx} \lt 0, so f has a local maximum.
At the point (6,2), we have D > 0 and f_{xx} > 0, so f has a local minimum.
At the point (6,-2), we have D \lt 0, so f has a saddle point.

Next, f_{yy} = f_{xx} = -6 (x+y)^2, and f_{xy} = 16 - 6(x+y)^2. The discriminant is D(x,y) = f_{xx}f_{yy}- f_{xy}^2, so D = 36(x+y)^4 - \left(16 - 6(x + y)^2\right)^2. Thus D(0,0) = -256 \lt 0, so (0,0) is a saddle point.

static.solution: f_x(x,y) = 32 x^3 and f_y(x,y) = -2y e^{-y^2}. These will vanish simultaneously when x=0 and y=0, so our only critical point is (0,0). The discriminant is D=f_{xx}(x,y)f_{yy}(x,y)-f_{xy}^2(x,y) = (96 x^2)(-2 e^{-y^2} + 4y^2 e^{-y^2}) - (0)^2. Unfortunately, the discriminant is zero at the origin so the second derivative test can tell us nothing about our critical point. We can, however, see that we are at a saddle point by looking at the behavior of f(x,y) along the x and y axes. Along the x axis we have f(x,0) = 8 x^4 + 1, which has f(x,0) > f(0,0) = 1 for x \ne 0; but along the y axis, f(0,y) = e^{-y^2}, for which f(0,y) \lt f(0,0) = 1 for y\ne 0. Thus f(x,y) has neither a maximum nor a minimum at (0,0).

For y\to-\infty, and as x\to\pm\infty, we have the same behavior. So we could have a global minimum. We can check this by finding the critical points and testing them: f_x = x - 6, and f_y = 32\,y^3 + 12 y = 2y(16 y^2 + 6), so the only critical point is (6,0). statement.p: A closed rectangular box with faces parallel to the coordinate planes has one bottom corner at the origin and the opposite top corner in the first octant on the plane 2 x + 6 y + z = 1. What is the maximum volume of such a box?
volume =

static.solution:
(x,y,z), the volume of the box is V=xyz. Since z=1 - 2 x - 6 y on the plane, the volume is given by V=xy (1 - 2 x - 6 y) = xy - 2 x^2 y - 6 xy^2. The domain is the triangular region 0\leq x\leq \frac{1}{2}, 0\leq y \leq (1 - 2 x)/6. At a critical point, \frac{\partial V}{\partial x} = y - 4 xy - 6 y^2 = y(1- x- 6 y) = 0, and \frac{\partial V}{\partial y} = x - 2 x^2 - 12 xy = x(1 - 2 x- 12 y) = 0. One solution is x=y=0. Another is x=0, y=\frac{1}{6}; another is y=0, x=\frac{1}{2}. Another is the solution of 1 - 4 x - 6 y = 0, \qquad 1 - 2 x - 12 y =0, namely x=\frac{1}{6}, y=\frac{1}{18}.
If either x=0 or y=0, then V=0, so these solutions do not give the maximum volume. Since D=V_{xx}V_{yy}-(V_{xy})^2 = (-4 y)(-12 x) - (1 - 4 x - 12 y)^2, at the remaining critical point we have D\left ( \frac{1}{6}, \frac{1}{18}\right ) = \left(-4 \cdot\frac1{18}\right) \left(-12\cdot\frac1{6}\right) - \left(1 - 4\cdot\frac1{6} - 12\cdot\frac1{18}\right)^2 = \frac{4}{9}-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{1}{3}>0, and V_{xx}(\frac1{6},\frac1{18})=-\frac{2}{9}\lt 0, the point x=\frac{1}{6},\, y=\frac{1}{18}, is a local maximum at which V= (1/6)(1/18) - 2(1/6)^2(1/18) - 6(1/6)(1/18)^2 = 1/324.
Since all points on the boundary of the domain give V=0, the local maximum is a global maximum.

Use the Second Derivative Test to determine whether the point is
a local maximum
