a local minimum
test fails

static.solution:
f(x,y)=x^{2}+y^{2}+xy+6x equal to zero and solve f_x(x,y)=2x+y+6=0 f_y(x,y)=2y+x=0 The second equation implies that y=-0.5x. Substituting into the first and solving for x gives: 2x - 0.5x+6=0 \Rightarrow x=-4 The corresponding value of y is y=-0.5(-4)=2. The critical point is (-4,2).
Now we compute the Discriminant. We find the second-order partials: f_{xx}(x,y)=2 \quad f_{yy}(x,y)=2 \quad f_{xy}(x,y)=1 The discriminant is D(x,y)=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2=2\cdot 2-(1)^2=3
Applying the Second Derivative Test we have D(-4,2)=3 > 0 \quad f_{xx}(-4,2)=2>0 The Second Derivative test implies that f(-4,2) is a local minimum.

statement.p: Find the critical points of the function f(x,y)=x^{4}+y^{4}-144xy
Answer :
Starting with the point with the smallest x value, use the Second Derivative Test to determine whether each critical point is

static.solution:
f(x,y)=x^{4}+y^{4}-144xy equal to zero and solve f_x(x,y)=4x^{3}-144y=0 f_y(x,y)=4y^{3}-144x=0 The first equation implies that y=\frac{4x^{3}}{144}. Substituting into the second and solving for x gives: 4\left(\frac{4x^{3}}{144}\right)^{3} - 144 x=144 x\left(\frac{4^4}{144^4}x^8-1\right)=0 \Rightarrow x=0, x=\pm 6 The corresponding y coordinates are y=0 \quad y=\pm 6 critical points are (0,0),(6,6), (-6,-6).
Now we compute the Discriminant. We find the second-order partials: f_{xx}(x,y)=12x^2 \quad f_{yy}(x,y)=12y^2 \quad f_{xy}(x,y)=-144 The discriminant is thus D(x,y)=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2=144x^{2}y^{2}-20736
Applying the Second Derivative Test we have D(0,0)=-20736\lt 0 D(6,6)=165888>0 \quad f_{xx}(6,6)=432>0 D(-6,-6)=165888>0 \quad f_{xx}(-6,-6)=432>0 We conclude that f(0,0) is a saddle point, whereas f(6,6) and f(-6,-6) are local minima.

statement.p: Find the critical point of the function f(x,y)=5e^{x}-3xe^{y}.

Use the Second Derivative Test to determine whether it is
a local minimum
test fails
a saddle point
a local maximum

static.solution:
f(x,y)=5e^{x}-3xe^{y} equal to zero and solve f_x(x,y)=5e^{x}-3e^{y}=0 f_y(x,y)=-3xe^{y}=0 Since e^y\ne 0, the second equation gives x=0. Substituting in the first equation, we get: 5 e^0-3 e^y=0 \Rightarrow y=\ln (5/3)=0.510826
Now we compute the Discriminant. We find the second-order partials: f_{xx}(x,y)=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(5e^{x}-3e^{y}\right)=5e^{x} f_{yy}(x,y)=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(-3xe^{y}\right)=-3xe^{y} f_{xy}(x,y)=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(5e^{x}-3e^{y}\right)=-3e^{y} The discriminant is thus D(x,y)=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2=-\left(15xe^{x+y}+9e^{2y}\right)
Applying the Second Derivative Test we have D(0,0.510826)=-25\lt 0 We conclude that f(0,0.510826) is a saddle point.

statement.p: Find the critical point of the function f(x,y)=-\left(12x+2y^{2}+\ln\mathopen{}\left(\left|x+y\right|\right)\right).

Use the Second Derivative Test to determine whether it is
a local minimum
a saddle point
a local maximum
test fails

static.solution:
f(x,y)=-\left(12x+2y^{2}+\ln\mathopen{}\left(\left|x+y\right|\right)\right) equal to zero and solve f_x(x,y)=-\left(12+\frac{1}{x+y}\right)=0 f_y(x,y)=-\left(4y+\frac{1}{x+y}\right)=0 The first equation implies that \frac{1}{x+y}=-12. Substituting into the second equation gives 12-4y=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad y=3 We substitute y=3 in the first equation and solve for x: -12-\frac{1}{x+3}=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x+3=\frac{1}{-12} \quad \Rightarrow \quad x=\frac{-3 \cdot -12 + 1}{-12}=\frac{37}{-12} We obtain critical point \left(\frac{37}{-12}, 3\right).
Notice, that although f_x and f_y do not exist where x+y=0, these are not critical points, since f is not defined at these points.
Now we compute the Discriminant. We find the second-order partials: f_{xx}(x,y)=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(-\left(12+\frac{1}{x+y}\right)\right)=\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}} f_{yy}(x,y)=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(-\left(4y+\frac{1}{x+y}\right)\right)=\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}}-4 f_{xy}(x,y)=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(-\left(12+\frac{1}{x+y}\right)\right)=\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}} The discriminant is thus D(x,y)=f_{xx}f_{yy}-f_{xy}^2=\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}} \cdot \left(\frac{1}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}}-4\right)-\frac{1}{(x+y)^4}=-\frac{4}{\left(x+y\right)^{2}}
Applying the Second Derivative Test we have D\left(\frac{37}{-12},3\right)=-576\lt 0 We conclude that f\left(\frac{37}{-12},3\right) is a saddle point.

statement.p: Determine the global extreme values of the function f(x,y)=x^{3}-5y, \quad 0 \le x,y \le 1

static.solution:
f_x(x,y)=3x^{2}=0, \quad f_y(x,y)=-5 The two equations have no solutions, hence there are no critical points.
The extreme values occur either at the critical points or at a point on the boundary of the domain.
To check the boundary we consider each edge of the square 0\le x,y \le 1 separately.
The segment \mathrm{OA}: On this segment y=0, 0\le x\le 1, and f takes the values f(x,0)=x^{3}.
The minimum value is f(0,0)=0 and the maximum value is f(1,0)=1.
The segment \mathrm{AB}: On this segment x=1, 0\le y\le 1, and f takes the values f(1,y)=1-5y.
The minimum value is f(1,1)=-4 and the maximum value is f(1,0)=1.
The segment \mathrm{BC}: On this segment y=1, 0\le x\le 1, and f takes the values f(x,1)=x^{3}-5.
The minimum value is f(0,1)=-5 and the maximum value is f(1,1)=-4.
The segment \mathrm{OC}: On this segment x=0, 0\le y\le 1, and f takes the values f(0,y)=-5y.
The minimum value is f(0,1)=-5 and the maximum value is f(0,0)=0.
The smallest value is f_{min}=-5 and it is the global minimum of f on the square.
The global maximum is the largest value f_{max}=1.

statement.p: Determine the global extreme values of the function f(x,y)=2x^{3}+2x^{2}y+y^{2}, \quad x,y \ge 0, x+y \le 1

static.solution:
f_x(x,y)=6x^{2}+4xy=x\mathopen{}\left(6x+4y\right)=0 f_y(x,y)=2x^{2}+2y=0 The first equation gives x=0 or y=-1.5x.
Substituting x=0 in the second equation gives 2 y=0 or y=0.
We obtain the critical point (0,0). We now substitute y=-1.5x in the second equation and solve for x: 2x^{2}-3x=x\mathopen{}\left(2x-3\right)=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x=0, x=1.5 We get the critical points (0,0), (1.5,-2.25).
None of the critical points is in the interior of the domain.
We check the boundary. The boundary consists of the three segments \mathrm{OA},\mathrm{OB} and \mathrm{AB} shown in the figure.
We consider each part of the boundary separately.
The segment \mathrm{OA}: On this segment y=0, 0\le x\le 1, and f(x,y)=f(x,0)=2x^{3}.
The minimum value is f(0,0)=0 and the maximum value is f(1,0)=2.
The segment \mathrm{OB}: On this segment x=0, 0\le y\le 1, and f(x,y)=f(0,y)=y^{2}.
The minimum value is f(0,0)=0 and the maximum value is f(1,0)=1.
The segment \mathrm{AB}: On this segment y=1-x, 0\le x\le 1, and f(x,1-x)=2x^{3}+2x^{2}\mathopen{}\left(1-x\right)+\left(1-x\right)^{2}=3x^{2}-2x+1
We find extreme values of g(x)=3x^{2}-2x+1 in the interval 0\le x\le 1.
Setting g'(x)=0 we find g'(x)=6x-2=0 \quad \Rightarrow \quad x=\frac{1}{3} g\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)=0.666667, \quad g(0)=1, \quad g(1)=2
In conclusion, we find that the global minimum of f on the given domain is f_{min}=0 and the global maximum f_{max}=2

statement.p: Use Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum and minimum values of f(x,y) = 2 x - 5 y subject to the constraint x^2 + 3 y^2 = 111, if such values exist.
maximum =
minimum =

p.em: (For either value, enter DNE if there is no such value.)

static.solution: f(x,y)= 2 x - 5 y and our equation of constraint is g(x,y) = x^2 + 3 y^2 = 111. To optimize f(x,y) with Lagrange multipliers we solve the following system of equations f_{x}(x,y) = \lambda g_{x}(x,y),\qquad\mbox{so } 2 = 2\lambda x, f_{y}(x,y) = \lambda g_{y}(x,y),\qquad\mbox{so } -5 = 6\lambda y, and g(x,y) = 111,\qquad\mbox{so } x^2 + 3 y^2 = 111. Solving for \lambda gives us \lambda = \frac{1}{ x} = \frac{-5}{6 y}, which we can use to find x in terms of y: x = -\frac{6}{5}\,y. Using this relation in our equation of constraint, we can solve for y: x^2 + 3 y^2 = 111, so (-\frac{6}{5}\, y)^2 + 3 y^2 = 111, and thus ((\frac{6}{5})^2 + 3)\, y^2 = 111. So, solving for y, we have y = \pm 5, and x = \mp 6. Thus, the critical points are (-6,5) and (6,-5). Since the constraint is closed and bounded, maximum and minimum values of f subject to the constraint exist. Evaluating f at the critical points, we find that the maximum value is f(6,-5) = 2(6) + 5(5) = 37 and the minimum value is f(-6,5) = -2(6) - 5(5) = -37.

statement.p: Use Lagrange multipliers to find the maximum and minimum values of f(x,y) = x^2 y + 3 y^2 - y, subject to the constraint x^2 + y^2 \leq 10
maximum =
minimum =

p.em: (For either value, enter DNE if there is no such value.)

static.solution:
f: f_x = 2xy = 0, \quad f_y = x^2 + 6 y - 1 = 0. From the first equation, we get either x=0 or y=0. If x=0, from the second equation we get 6 y - 1 = 0, so y=1/6. If instead y=0, then from the second equation x=\pm 1. We conclude that the critical points are (0,1/6), (1,0), and (-1,0). All three critical points satisfy the constraint x^2+y^2\le 10.
The Lagrange conditions, \nabla f= \lambda\nabla g, are: 2xy=\lambda 2x,\qquad x^2 + 6 y - 1 =\lambda 2y. From the first equation, when x\neq 0, we divide by 2x to get \lambda=y. Substituting into the second equation, we get x^2 + 6 y - 1 = 2y^2. Then using x^2 = 10 - y^2 from the constraint, we have 10 - y^2 + 6 y - 1 = 2 y^2, so 3 y^2 - 6 y - 9 = 0. Factoring, we get (3y + 3 )( y - 3 ) = 0, so y = -1 or y = 3. From the constraint, we get x=\pm 3 when y=-1 and x=\pm 1 for y=3.
If instead x=0, so that we cannot divide by x in the first Lagrange equation, then from the constraint, y=\pm \sqrt{10}.
Summarizing, the following points are either critical points or satisfy the Lagrange conditions: (\pm 1,0),(0,1/6),(\pm 3, -1),(\pm 1, 3), (0, -\sqrt{10}), \mbox{ and } (0, \sqrt{10}). These are the candidates for global maximum or minimum points. The corresponding values for f(x,y)=x^2 y + 3 y^2 - y are: 0, -0.083, -5, 27, 33.162, \mbox{ and } 26.838. The largest value is 33.1623 at the point (0,-\sqrt{10}), and the smallest value is -5 at (\pm 3,-1),

Find the minimum distance from the point (1,5,12) to the paraboloid given by the equation z=x^2+y^2.
Minimum distance =

Note: If you need to find roots of a polynomial of degree \geq 3, you may want to use a calculator of computer to do so numerically. Also be sure that you can give a geometric justification for your answer.

static.solution:
(x,y,z) be a point on the paraboloid. The square of the distance from (x,y,z) to the point (1,5,12) is given by f(x,y,z) = (x-1)^2 + (y-5)^2 + (z-12)^2, and so we wish to minimize f(x,y,z) subject to the constraint g(x,y,z) = x^2+y^2-z = 0. We look for solutions to the equations \nabla f = \lambda\nabla g and g=0: 2(x-1) = 2\lambda x, 2(y-5) = 2\lambda y, 2(z-12) = -\lambda, and x^2+y^2-z = 0. If \lambda=0, the first three equations would imply that (x,y,z)=(1,5,12), which does not satisfy the fourth equation and so \lambda\ne 0. If collect terms in x and y in the first and second equations, respectively, we get (1 - \lambda) x = 1, and (1 - \lambda) y = 5. Note that we cannot have \lambda = 1, x = 0 or y = 0, and so can divide these two equation to solve for y, getting y = 5 x.
If we divide the first and third equations we got from the Lagrange multipliers method, we have \frac{x - 1}{z - 12} = -2x, so that z = 12 - \frac12(1 - \frac{1}{x}).
We can then plug all of these into the last equation, the constraint. This gives x^2 + 25 x^2 - 12 + \frac12(1 - \frac{1}{x}) = 0. Multiplying by x and collecting terms, we have 52 x^3 - 23 x - 1 = 0. Let h(x) = 52 x^3 - 23 x - 1. Clearly h(-3) \lt 0, h(-\frac12) > 0, h(0) \lt 0 and h(3) > 0. Thus there must be roots lying between x = -3 and x = -0.5, between x = -0.5 and x = 0, and between x = 0 and x = 3. We can locate these numerically using a calculator or computer program, to find x = -0.642152907, \quad x = -0.04366650472, \quad\mbox{and}\quad x = 0.685819412. Then, using the equations for y and z in terms of x, we have the corresponding values of y and z, and therefore have three solutions to the Lagrange multiplier equations: x_1 = -0.642152907, y_1 = -3.210764535, z_1 = 10.7213692551823, x_2 = -0.04366650472, y_2 = -0.2183325236, z_2 = 0.0495758544960063, and x_3 = 0.685819412, y_3 = 3.42909706, z_3 = 12.2290549127767.
The distances (squared) from the paraboloid are d_1 = d(x_1,y_1,z_1) = 71.7482170007753, d_2 = d(x_2,y_2,z_2) = 171.132871357381, and d_3 = d(x_3,y_3,z_3) = 2.6189116418438, so that the minimum distance is \sqrt{d_3} = 1.61831.
Note that the geometric interpretation of this is that it is the length of a perpendicular line segment drawn from the paraboloid to the point.

statement.p: For each value of \lambda the function h(x,y) = x^2 + y^2 - \lambda(6 x + 2 y - 19) has a minimum value m(\lambda).
(a) Find m(\lambda)

p.em: (Use the letter L for \lambda in your expression.)

statement.p: (b) For which value of \lambda is m(\lambda) the largest, and what is that maximum value?
maximum m(\lambda) =
(c) Find the minimum value of f(x,y)=x^2+y^2 subject to the constraint 6 x + 2 y = 19 using the method of Lagrange multipliers and evaluate \lambda.
minimum f =

p.em: (How are these results related to your result in part (b)?)

static.solution:
(a) The critical points of h(x,y) occur where h_x(x,y) = 2 x - 6 \lambda = 0 and h_y(x,y) = 2 y - 2 \lambda = 0. The only critical point is (x,y) = (3 \lambda, \lambda) and it gives a minimum value for h(x,y). That minimum value is m(\lambda) = h(3 \lambda, \lambda) = 9 \lambda^2 + \lambda^2 - \lambda( 18 \lambda + 2 \lambda - 19 ) or m(\lambda) = -10 \lambda^2 + 19 \lambda.
(b) The maximum value of m(\lambda)= -10 \lambda^2 + 19\lambda occurs at a critical point, where m'(\lambda) = -20 \lambda + 19 = 0. At this point, \lambda = 0.95 and m(0.95)= 9.025.
(c) We want to minimize f(x,y)=x^2+y^2 subject to the constraint g(x,y)=19, where g(x,y) = 6 x + 2 y. The method of Lagrange multipliers has us solve 2x = 6\lambda, 2y = 2\lambda, and 6 x + 2 y = 19. We can see that this gives the same solutions for x and y as we obtained in part (a), and then, plugging in to the third equation, we have 18 \lambda + 2 \lambda = 19. Thus we get the same \lambda as before: \lambda = 0.95, so that the minimum value of f is f(3\lambda, \lambda), where \lambda = 0.95, or f_{\mbox{min}} = 9.025.
Note that the two question have the same answer. This makes sense, because in the first problem the largest minimum value will clearly occur when 6 x + 2 y = 19, which is the constraint in the third equation.

(a) If \sum_{i=1}^3 x_i = 3, find the values of x_1, x_2, x_3 making \sum_{i=1}^3 {x_i}^2 minimum.

p.em: (Give your values as a comma separated list.)

statement.p: (b) Generalize the result of part (a) to find the minimum value of \sum_{i=1}^n{x_i}^2 subject to \sum_{i=1}^n x_i=3.
minimum value =

static.solution:
(a) Let f(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\sum_{i=1}^3{x_i}^2 = {x_1}^2 + {x_2}^2 + {x_3}^2 and g(x_1,x_2,x_3)=\sum_{i=1}^3 x_i = 3. Then \nabla f = \lambda\nabla g gives 2x_1 = \lambda = 2x_2 = 2x_3. so x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = \frac{\lambda}2. Then x_1+x_2+x_3 = 3 gives 3\frac{\lambda}{2} = 3\quad\hbox{ so } \quad \lambda = 2. Thus x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 1.
These values of x_1, x_2,x_3 give the minimum (rather than maximum) because the value of without bound as x_2,x_2,x_3\to\infty.
(b) A similar argument shows that \sum_{i=1}^nx_i has its minimum value subject to \sum_{i=1}^nx_i = 3 when x_1=x_2=\cdots= x_n=\frac{3}n. Then the minimum value is \sum_1^n \left(\frac{3}{n}\right)^2 = n\cdot \left(\frac{3}{n}\right)^2 = \frac{9}{n}.

Let R be the rectangle with vertices (0,0), (8,0), (8,8), and (0,8) and let f(x,y) = \sqrt{0.5xy}.
(a) Find reasonable upper and lower bounds for \int_{R}f\,dA without subdividing R.
upper bound =
lower bound =

(b) Estimate \int_{R}f\,dA three ways: by partitioning R into four subrectangles and evaluating f at its maximum and minimum values on each subrectangle, and then by considering the average of these (over and under) estimates.
overestimate: \int_{R}f\,dA \approx
underestimate: \int_{R}f\,dA \approx
average: \int_{R}f\,dA \approx

static.solution:
(a) If we take the partition of R consisting of just R itself, we get \mbox{Lower bound }= \mbox{min}_R f\cdot A_R=0\cdot (8-0)(8-0)=0. Similarly, we get \mbox{Upper bound } = \hbox{max}_R f\cdot A_R = \frac{8}{\sqrt2}\cdot (8-0)(8-0)=\frac{512}{\sqrt2}.
(b) The estimates asked for are just the upper and lower sums. We partition R into subrectangles R_{(a,b)} of width 4 and height 4, where (a,b) is the lower-left corner of R_{(a,b)}. The subrectangles are then R_{(0,0)}, R_{(4,0)}, R_{(0,2)}, and R_{(2,2)}. Then we find the lower sum \mbox{Lower } =\sum_{(a,b)}A_{R_{(a,b)}}\cdot\min_{R_{(a,b)}}f = \sum_{(a,b)} 16\cdot (\mbox{Min of }f \mbox{ on }R_{(a,b)}). The minimum occurs at the lower-left corner of each rectangle, so \mbox{Lower } = 16\cdot( f(0,0) + f(4,0) + f(0,4) + f(4,4) ) = 512.
Similarly, the upper sum is \mbox{Upper } = 16\sum_{(a,b)}(\mbox{Max of }f \mbox{ on }R_{(a,b)}), so \mbox{Upper } = 16(f(2,2)+f(4,2)+f(2,4)+f(4,4)) = 64(\frac3{\sqrt2} + 2). The upper sum is an overestimate and the lower sum is an underestimate, so we can get a better estimate by averaging them to get 64(\sqrt2 + 1).

statement.p: Using Riemann sums with four subdivisions in each direction, find upper and lower bounds for the volume under the graph of f(x,y) = 5+3xy above the rectangle R with 0\le x\le 4,\quad 0\le y \le 6.
upper bound =
lower bound =

static.solution:
R into subrectangles with the lines x=0, x=1, x=2, x=3, and x=4 and the lines y=0, y=1.5, y=3, y=4.5, and y=6. Then we have 16 subrectangles, each of which we denote R_{(a,b)}, where (a,b) is the location of the lower-left corner of the subrectangle.
We want to find a lower bound and an upper bound for the volume above each subrectangle. The lower bound for the volume of R_{(a,b)} is 1.5 ( \mbox{Min of } f \mbox{ on } R_{(a,b)}) because the area of R_{(a,b)} is 1\cdot 1.5=1.5. The function f(x,y) = 5+3xy increases with both x and y over the whole region R. Thus, \mbox{Min of } f \mbox{ on } R_{(a,b)} = f(a,b) = 5+3ab, because the minimum on each subrectangle is at the corner closest to the origin.
Similarly, \mbox{Max of } f \mbox{ on } R_{(a,b)} = f(a+1,b+1.5) = 5 + 3(a+1)(b+1.5). So we have \mbox{Lower sum } = \sum_{(a,b)} 1.5(5+3ab) = 1.5 \sum_{(a,b)} 5+3ab = 120 + 1.5\sum_{(a,b)}3 ab Since a=0, 1, 2, 3 and b= 0, 1.5, 3, 4.5, expanding this sum gives \mbox{Lower} = 120 + 1.5 (0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 4.5 + 9 + 13.5 + 0 + 9 + 18 + 27 + 0 + 13.5 + 27 + 40.5) = 363.
Similarly, we can compute the upper sum: \mbox{Upper sum }= \sum_{(a,b)}1.5(5+3(a+1)(b+1.5)) = 1.5\sum_{(a,b)}(5+3(a+1)(b+1.5)) = 120 + 1.5\sum_{(a,b)}(a+1)(b+1.5) = 795.

statement.p: Using Riemann sums, estimate the average temperature in the room.
average temperature =

static.solution:
\Delta A=1.
We shall begin our sum as an upper estimate starting with the lower left corner of the room and continue across the bottom and moving upward using the highest temperature, T_i, in each case. So the upper Riemann sum becomes \sum_{i=1}^{25} T_i \Delta A = T_1 \Delta A + T_2 \Delta A + T_3 \Delta A + \cdots + T_{25} \Delta A = \Delta A (T_1 + T_2 + T_3 + \cdots + T_{25}). Thus, taking the maximum value for each region (and, where the temperatures are not bounded in the box, taking the largest value plus one), we have \mbox{sum} = (1)(21 + 22 + 22 + 23 + 23 + 22 + 23 + 23 + 23 + 24 + 24 + 24 + 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 + 26 + 26 + 26 + 26 + 27 + 28 + 29 + 28 + 27) = 617.
In the same way, the lower Riemann sum is formed by taking the lowest temperature (and, where the temperatures are not bounded in the box, taking the largest value minus one), t_i, in each case: \sum_{i=1}^{25} t_i \Delta A = t_1 \Delta A + t_2 \Delta A + t_3 \Delta A + \cdots + t_{25} \Delta A = \Delta A (t_1 + t_2 + t_3 + \cdots + t_{25}). Thus, taking the minimum value for each region, we have \mbox{sum} = (1)(18 + 20 + 21 + 22 + 22 + 20 + 21 + 22 + 22 + 23 + 22 + 22 + 23 + 23 + 23 + 23 + 24 + 24 + 25 + 25 + 24 + 25 + 26 + 26 + 25) = 571.
So, averaging the upper and lower sums we get: 594.
To compute the average temperature, we divide by the area of the room, \mbox{Average temperature} = \frac{594}{25} = 23.76. That is, approximately 23.76^{\circ}C.

static.solution:
(a) The contour f(x,y)=1 lies in the xy-plane and has equation 8 e^{-(x-1)^2-y^2} = 1, so -(x-1)^2-y^2 = \ln (1/8),\quad\mbox{or}\quad (x-1)^2+y^2 = \ln 8. This is the equation of a circle of radius \sqrt{\ln(8)} centered at (1,0) in the xy-plane. Similarly, for k \lt 8, we have that the contours f(x,y) = k are the circles (x - 1)^2 + y^2 = \ln(8/k), all of which are centered on (1,0).
(b) The cross-section has equation z=f(1,y)=8 e^{-y^2}. If x=1, the base region in the xy-plane extends from y=-\sqrt{3} to y=\sqrt{3}. Thus the area is \hbox{Area } = \int_{-\sqrt{3}}^{\sqrt{3}}8 e^{-y^2}\,dy.
(c) Using this idea and slicing parallel to the y-axis, we get \hbox{Volume } = \int_{-2}^{2}\int_{-\sqrt{4-x^2}}^{\sqrt{4-x^2}} 8 e^{-(x-1)^2-y^2}\,dy\,dx.

statement.p: Then, for the region R given by 0 \le x \le 2, 0 \le y \le 5, what constant function p(x,y) is a joint density function?

static.solution:
(a) p is not a joint density function. Since p(x,y)=0 outside the region R, the volume under the graph of p is the same as the volume under the graph of p over the region R, which is 12, not one, which it would have to be if p(x,y) were a joint density function..
(b) p is a joint density function. Since p(x,y)=0 outside the region R, the volume under the graph of p is the same as the volume under the graph of p over the region R, which is 1, which is the value it must have if p(x,y) is a joint density function..
Finally, for a constant function to be a joint density function on R given by 0 \le x \le 2, 0 \le y \le 5, the volume under the constant must be one. So, if p(x,y) = k, 10 k = 1, so p(x,y) = \frac1{10}.

statement.p: probability =
(b) x \lt \frac{1}{6} + y:
probability =

static.solution:
(a) The probability is \int_0^1\int_{1/6}^1 {2 \over 3} (x + 2y) \,dx\,dy = \int_0^1 {2\over3} ({1\over2}x^2 + 2xy)\bigr|^1_{1/6}\,dy = \int_0^1 {2\over3} \left[({1\over2} + 2y) - ({1\over 72} + {\frac{1}{3}}y)\right]\,dy = {2\over3}\int_0^1 (\frac{35}{72} + \frac{5}{3} y) \, dy = {2\over3} \left(\frac{35}{72} y + \frac{5}{6} y^2\right)\bigr|_0^1 = {2\over3} \left(\frac{95}{72}\right) = \frac{95}{108}.
(b) It is easier to calculate the probability that x \lt \frac1{6} + y does not happen, that is, the probability that x \ge \frac1{6} + y, and subtract it from 1. The probability that x \ge \frac1{6} + y is \int_{0}^{5/6}\int_{y+1/6}^{1} {2\over3} (x+2y) \,dx\,dy = \int_{0}^{5/6} (\frac13\,x^2 + \frac43\,xy) \bigr|_{y+(1/6)}^{1} \,dy = \int_{0}^{5/6} \frac13\left(1 - (\frac1{6} + y)^2\right) + \frac43(y)(1 - (\frac1{6} + y)) \,dy = \int_{0}^{5/6} -\frac53\,y^2 + y + \frac{35}{108} \, dy = (-\frac59\,y^3 + \frac{1}{2}\, y^2 + \frac{35}{108}\,y)\bigr|_{0}^{5/6} = \frac{575}{1944}. Thus, the probability that x \lt \frac1{6}+y is 1-(\frac{575}{1944}) = \frac{1369}{1944}.

static.solution: -\pi/4\le\theta\le\pi/4. Also, the outer (right) boundary of the region is \sqrt{10} = x = r\cos\theta. Hence, 0\le r\le \sqrt{10}/\cos\theta. The integral becomes \int_0^{\sqrt{10}}\int_{-x}^x\,dy\,dx =\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\int_0^{\sqrt{10}/\!\cos\theta}\,r\,dr\,d\theta. Then \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\int_0^{\sqrt{10}/\!\cos\theta}\,r\,dr\,d\theta = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(\frac{r^2}{2}\bigg|_0^{\sqrt{10}/\!\cos\theta}\right)\,d\theta = \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{5}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta. And \int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{5}{\cos^2\theta}\,d\theta =5 \tan\theta\bigg|_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4} = 5\cdot(1 - (-1)) = 10. Notice that we can check this answer because the integral gives the area of the shaded triangular region which is \frac{1}{2} \cdot \sqrt{10} \cdot (2\sqrt{10}) = 10.

mass =

static.solution:
z = 9 - 3 x - 3 y. Note that the projection of this into the xy-plane is the triangular region below y = 3 - x.
The mass of the volume is then M = \int_R \delta\,dV = \int_0^3\int_0^{3 - x}\int_0^{9-3 x-3 y}\,x + 3 y\,dz\,dy\,dx. Integrating with respect to z, M = \int_0^3\int_0^{3 - x} (x + 3 y)(9-3 x-3 y)\,dy\,dx so that M = \int_0^3\int_0^{3 - x} -3 x^2 + 9 x - 3 x y - 9 x y + 27 y - 9 y^2\,dy\,dx. Then, integrating with respect to y, M = \int_0^3 (-3 x^2 + 9 x)(3 - x) + \frac12(27 - 12 x)(3 - x)^2 - 3 (3 - x)^3\,dx. Expanding the these terms, we have M = \int_0^3 0 x^3 + \frac{9}{2} x^2 - 27 x + \frac{81}{2}\, dx = \frac{81}{2}.

statement.p: The moment of inertia of a solid body about an axis in 3-space relates the angular acceleration about this axis to torque (force twisting the body). The moments of inertia about the coordinate axes of a body of constant density and mass m occupying a region W of volume V are defined to be I_x = \frac{m}{V}\int_W (y^2+z^2) \,dV\qquad I_y = \frac{m}{V}\int_W (x^2+z^2) \,dV\qquad I_z = \frac{m}{V}\int_W (x^2+y^2) \,dV
Use these definitions to find the moment of inertia about the z-axis of the rectangular solid of mass 48 given by 0 \le x \le 3, 0 \le y \le 2, 0 \le z \le 4.

static.solution:
V of the solid is 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 = 24. Thus for I_x we have I_x = \frac{48}{24}\int_W\, y^2 + z^2\,dV = 2\int_0^3\int_0^2\int_0^4\,y^2 + z^2\,dz\,dy\,dx. This is I_x = 2\int_0^3\int_0^2 y^2 z + \frac13 z^3\bigg|_{z=0}^{z=4} = 2\int_0^{3}\int_0^{2}\, 4 y^2 + \frac{64}{3}\, dy\,dx, or I_x = 2\int_0^3 \frac{32}{3} + \frac{128}{3}\, dx = 320.
Similarly, I_y = 400,\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad I_z = 208.

static.solution: \frac{\partial (x,y)}{\partial (s,t)} = \left|\begin{array}{ccc} x_s \amp x_t\\ y_s\amp y_t \end{array}\right| =\left|\begin{array}{ccc} 2 \amp 8 \\ 1 \amp 4 \end{array}\right| = 0. Therefore, \left|\frac{\partial (x,y)}{\partial (s,t)}\right|=0.

statement.p: Find the Jacobian. \frac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (s,t,u)}, where x = 2t-2s-4u, y = s-t+3u, z = -\left(5s+2t+4u\right).

static.solution: \left|\frac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (s,t,u)}\right| = \left|\begin{array}{ccc} x_s \amp x_t \amp x_u\\ y_s \amp y_t \amp y_u\\ z_s \amp z_t \amp z_u \end{array}\right| =\left|\begin{array}{ccc} -2 \amp 2 \amp -4\\ 1 \amp -1 \amp 3\\ -5 \amp -2 \amp -4 \end{array}\right|. This 3 \times 3 determinant is computed the same way as for the cross product, with the entries -2,2,-4 in the first row playing the same role as \vec i,\vec j,\vec k. We get \frac{\partial (x,y,z)}{\partial (s,t,u)}= ((-1)(-4)-(3)(-2))-2 + ((3)(-5)-(1)(-4))2 + ((1)(-2)-(-1)(-5))-4 = -14.

Use the change of variables s=y, t=y-x^2 to evaluate \int\int_R x \,dx\,dy over the region R in the first quadrant bounded by y=0, y=36, y=x^2, and y=x^2-5.

static.solution:
dA=\,dx\,dy, the integrand x and the region R.
Inverting the variable change gives x=\sqrt{s-t}, y=s where we use the positive square root because the region R is in the first quadrant where x\ge 0. Thus \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (s, t)}= \left\vert \begin{array}{cc}\frac{\partial x}{\partial s}\amp \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}\\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}\amp \frac{\partial y}{\partial t}\end{array}\right\vert =\left\vert \begin{array}{cc}1/(2\sqrt{s-t})\amp \quad -1/(2\sqrt{s-t})\\ 1\amp 0\end{array}\right\vert = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s-t}}. Therefore dx\,dy = \left\vert \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (s, t)}\right\vert \,ds\,dt =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{s-t}} \,ds\,dt.
The integrand is x = \sqrt{s-t}.
The region of integration can be transformed by examination of its boundaries. The left and right boundaries of R are given by y-x^2=t=0 and y-x^2 = t =-5. The bottom and top boundaries of given by y=s=0 and y=s=36.
Let T be the rectangle 0\le s\le 36, -5\le t \le 0 of area (5)(36)= 180. We have \int\int_R x\,dx\,dy= \int\int_T \sqrt{s-t}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{s-t}} \,ds\,dt= \frac{1}{2}(\hbox{Area of T}) = 90.

statement.p: Use the change of variables s = x + 3 y, t = y to find the area of the ellipse x^2 + 6 x y + 10 y^2 \le 1.
area =

static.solution:
\int\int_R \,dx\,dy where R is the region x^2 + 6 x y + 10 y^2\le 1. We must change variables in both the area element dA=\,dx\,dy and the region R.
Inverting the variable change gives x = s - 3 t, y = t. Thus \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (s, t)}= \left\vert \begin{array}{cc} \frac{\partial x}{\partial s}\amp \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}\\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s}\amp \frac{\partial y}{\partial t} \end{array} \right\vert = \left\vert \begin{array}{cr} 1 \amp -3\\ 0\amp 1 \end{array} \right\vert = 1. Therefore dx\,dy= \left\vert \frac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (s, t)}\right\vert \,ds\,dt = \,ds\,dt.
The region of integration is x^2 + 6 x y + 10 y^2 = (s - 3 t)^2+ 2(s - 3 t)t + 10 t^2 = s^2+t^2\le 1.
Let T be the unit disc s^2+t^2\le 1. We have \int\int_R \,dx\,dy= \int\int_T \,ds\,dt = \hbox{Area of }T = \pi.

statement.p: Use the change of variables s=xy, t=xy^2 to compute \int_R xy^2\,dA, where R is the region bounded by xy=4,\ xy=6,\ xy^2=4,\ xy^2=6.

static.solution:
\begin{array}{ccc}s\amp =\amp xy\\t\amp =\amp xy^2,\end{array}. we have \frac{\partial(s,t)}{\partial(x,y)}= \left| \begin{array}{ccc} \frac{\partial s}{\partial x} \amp \frac{\partial s}{\partial y}\\ \frac{\partial t}{\partial x} \amp \frac{\partial t}{\partial y} \end{array}\right| =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}y\amp x\\y^2\amp 2xy\end{array}\right|=xy^2=t. Since \frac{\partial(s,t)}{\partial(x,y)}\cdot \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}=1, \qquad \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}=\frac{1}{t}.
So \int_R xy^2\,dA=\int_{T}t\left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right|\,ds\,dt= \int_{T}t\,(\frac 1t)\,ds\,dt=\int_{T}\,ds\,dt, where T is the region bounded by s=4, s=6, t=4, t=6. Then \int_Rxy^2\,dA=\int_4^{6}\,ds\int_4^{6}\,dt=4.

statement.p: Find positive numbers a and b so that the change of variables s=ax, t=by transforms the integral \int\int_R \,dx\,dy into \int\int_T \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert \,ds\,dt for the region R, the rectangle 0\le x \le 75, 0\le y \le 70 and the region T, the square 0\le s, t \le 1.
What is \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert in this case?

static.solution:
T is defined by the inequalities 0 \le s = ax \le 1 \qquad 0\le t=by\le 1 that correspond to the inequalities 0\le x \le 1/a = 75 \qquad 0\le y \le 1/b = 70 that define R. Thus a=1/75 and b=1/70.
Then, we have x = 75 s and y = 70 t, so \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert = \left|\begin{array}{cc} 75 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 70 \end{array}\right| = 5250.

statement.p: Find a number a so that the change of variables s=x+ay, t=y transforms the integral \int\int_R \,dx\,dy over the parallelogram R in the xy-plane with vertices (0,0), (30,0), (-36,14), (-6,14) into an integral \int\int_T \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert\,ds\,dt over a rectangle T in the st-plane.
What is \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert in this case?

static.solution:
x = s-at, y=t. The four edges of R are y=0, y=14, y=-\frac{7}{18} x, y=-\frac{7}{18} (x-30). The change of variables transforms the edges to t=0, t=14, t=-\frac{7}{18} s + \frac{7}{18} at, t=-\frac{7}{18} s + \frac{7}{18} at + \frac{35}{3}. These are equations for the edges of a rectangle in the st-plane if the last two are of the form: s=(\hbox{Constant}). This happens when the t terms drop out, or a=\frac{18}{7}. With a=\frac{18}{7} the change of variables gives \int\int_T \left\vert \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert \,ds\,dt over the rectangle T: 0\le t \le 14, 0\le s\le 30.
The jacobian \left\vert\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert is \left\vert\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right\vert = \left\vert\begin{array}{cc} 1 \amp -\frac{18}{7} \\ 0 \amp 1 \end{array} \right\vert = 1.

static.solution:
\begin{array}{ccc} x \amp = \amp 2 s + t\\ y \amp = \amp s - 2 t, \end{array} we have \left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right| = \left|\begin{array}{cc} \frac{\partial x}{\partial s} \amp \frac{\partial x}{\partial t}\\ \frac{\partial y}{\partial s} \amp \frac{\partial y}{\partial t} \end{array}\right| =\left|\begin{array}{cc} 2 \amp 1 \\ 1 \amp -2 \end{array}\right| = |-5|, hence \left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right| = 5. We therefore get \int_R (x+y) \,dA = \int_{T} ((2 s + t) + (s - 2 t)) \left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}\right|dsdt = \int_{T}(3s-t)(5)\,ds\,dt=\int_{T} (5\mathopen{}\left(3s-t\right))\,ds\,dt, where T is the region in the st-plane corresponding to R.
Now, we need to find T.
Because \begin{array}{ccc} x \amp = \amp 2 s+ t \\ y \amp = \amp s - 2 t \end{array} we can use the boundaries of the region R to find the boundaries of T. Using the four vertices of the parallelogram R, we the edges y = \frac1{2}\,x, y = -2\,x, y = \frac{1}{2}\,(x-1) - 2 and y = -2(x - 2) + 1. So, from the above transformation, the boundaries are t = 0, s = 0, t = 1 and s = 1. Therefore \int_R(x+y)\,dA = \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1}\, 5\mathopen{}\left(3s-t\right) \,ds\,dt = 5. (Alternately, we could of course also write the integral as \int_{1}^{0} \int_{1}^{0}\, 5\mathopen{}\left(3s-t\right) \,ds\,dt.)

The line integral is then: \int_{\mathcal{C}} \mathbf{F} \cdot \,d\ \mathbf{r} = \int^1_0 \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{r}(t)) \cdot \mathbf{r} '(t) \ dt = \int^1_0 -18 t^2 \sin (3 t^3) - 2 t \cos ( t^2) + 12 t^4\ dt = \left [ 2 \cos (3 t^3) - 1 \sin ( t^2) + \frac{12}{5} t^5 \right ]^1_0 = 2 \cos (3) - 1 \sin (1) + \frac{2}{5}

static.solution: \vec F = (x^2+3 y)\vec i + y^3\vec j, the line integral along the third segment, which is parallel to the z-axis, is zero. On the first segment, which is parallel to the y-axis, only the \vec j-component contributes. On the second segment, which is parallel to the x-axis, only the \vec i-component contributes. On the first segment x=5 and y varies from 0 to 1; on the second segment y=1 and x varies from 5 to 0. statement.p: Find \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r for \vec F = 2 y\vec i - (\sin y)\vec j on the curve counterclockwise around the unit circle C starting at the point (1,0).

static.solution: C is parameterized by \vec r=\cos t\,\vec i+\sin t\,\vec j,\qquad\mbox{for } 0\le t\le 2\pi, so \vec F(t) = 2\sin t\,\vec i - \sin{(\sin t)}\,\vec j \quad \text{and} \quad \vec r\,'(t)=-\sin t\,\vec i + \cos t\,\vec j. Thus, \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_0^{2\pi} (2\sin t\,\vec i - \sin{(\sin t)}\,\vec j)\cdot (-\sin t\,\vec i+\,\cos t\,\vec j) dt =\int_0^{2\pi}(-2\sin^2 t - \sin{(\sin t)}\cos t) dt Using an identity to rewrite the first term, we get =\int_0^{2\pi}\bigg[-1(1-\cos 2t) - \sin{(\sin t)}\cos t\bigg] dt Integrating, using a substitution to integrate the last term in the integrand, we obtain: =\bigg[-1(t - \frac{1}{2} \sin 2t) +\cos{(\sin t)}\bigg]\bigg|_0^{2\pi} =-2\pi \quad \text {units of work}

static.solution: On C_1, only the \vec i-component of \vec F contributes to the integral. static.solution:
(a)\vec F is not a gradient vector field. If \vec F were a gradient vector field, then we would have \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = x\sqrt{2 x^2 + y^2 + z^2}, so that \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y} = x y(2 x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{-1/2}. But we also have that \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = y\sqrt{2 x^2 + y^2 + z^2}, so that \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\partial x} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y} = 2 x y(2 x^2 + y^2 + z^2)^{-1/2}. These two are not equal, which is a contradiction. Therefore \vec F cannot be a gradient vector field.
(b)\vec F is not a gradient vector field. If \vec F were a gradient vector field, then we would have \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 4 x y, so that \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y} = 4 x. But we also have that \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 4 y z, so that \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\partial x} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y} = 4 z. These two are not equal, which is a contradiction. Therefore \vec F cannot be a gradient vector field.
(c)\vec F is not a gradient vector field. If \vec F were a gradient vector field, then we would have \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = y, so that \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y} =. But we also have that \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = z, so that \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y\partial x} = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial y} = 0. These two are not equal, which is a contradiction. Therefore \vec F cannot be a gradient vector field.
(d)\vec F is a gradient vector field. By integrating the components of the vector field \vec F, we can see that f(x,y,z) = 5 x z is a potential function for \vec F.

static.solution: \int_{(0,0)}^{(1,0)}\vec F \cdot d\vec r by integrating from (0,0) to (1,0) by traversing the other three sides of the square with vertices (0,0), (1,0), (1,1) and (0,1). Thus \int_{(0,0)}^{(1,0)}\vec F \cdot d\vec r = \int_{(0,0)}^{(0,1)}\vec F \cdot d\vec r + \int_{(0,1)}^{(1,1)}\vec F \cdot d\vec r + \int_{(1,1)}^{(1,0)}\vec F \cdot d\vec r, so that \int_{(0,0)}^{(1,0)}\vec F \cdot d\vec r = \int_{(0,0)}^{(0,1)}\vec F \cdot d\vec r + \int_{(0,1)}^{(1,1)}\vec F \cdot d\vec r - \int_{(1,0)}^{(1,1)}\vec F \cdot d\vec r = 4.4 + 2.1 - 3.6 = 2.9.

statement.p: Let \vec r=x\,\vec i+y\,\vec j+z\,\vec k and \vec a = 4\,\vec i + 4\,\vec j + 2\,\vec k.

maximum value of \int_C\nabla(\vec r\cdot\vec a)\cdot d\vec r =

solution.p: SOLUTION
(a) Since \vec r\cdot\vec a = 4 x + 4 y + 2 z, we have \nabla(\vec r\cdot \vec a) = 4 \, \vec i + 4 \, \vec j + 2 \, \vec k=\vec a.
(b) By the Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals, we have \int_C\nabla(\vec r\cdot \vec a)\cdot d\vec r = \vec r\cdot \vec a\bigg|_{(0,0,0)}^{(a,b,c)} = \vec r_0\cdot \vec a = 4 a + 4 b + 2 c.

(c) Since \vec r_0\cdot \vec a=\|\vec r_0\| \|\vec a\|\cos\theta = 10\|\vec a\|\cos\theta, where \theta is the angle between \vec r_0 and \vec a, the maximum value of \vec r_0\cdot\vec a occurs if \vec r_0 is parallel to \vec a. Then \theta=0 and \int_C\nabla(\vec r\cdot\vec a)\cdot d\vec r = 10 \|\vec a\|\cos 0 = 10\sqrt{4^2 + 4^2 + 2^2} = 10\sqrt{36}.

statement.p: Find f if \nabla f=8xy\,\vec i+(4x^{2}+20y^{4})\,\vec j

static.solution: \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 8xy\quad\hbox{and}\quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 4x^{2}+20y^{4}. Now think of y as a constant in the equation for \partial f/\partial x and integrate, giving f(x,y) = 4 x^2y + C(y). Since the constant of integration may depend on y, it is written C(y). Differentiating this expression for f(x,y) with respect to y and using the fact that \partial f/\partial y = 4x^{2}+20y^{4}, we get \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 4 x^2 + C'(y) = 4x^{2}+20y^{4}. Therefore C'(y) = 20 y^{4}\quad\hbox{so}\quad C(y)=4 y^{5} + K. for some constant K. Thus, f(x,y) = 4x^{2}y+4y^{5}+K.

(b) Yes. We can find f by integrating \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} to find f. This gives f(x,y) = 3 x^2 + C(y), so that, differentiating again, we have \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 3 x^2 + C'(y). Thus we may take f(x,y) = 3x^{2}+y^{2}+K.

statement.p: Verify that \mathbf{F}=\nabla\varphi and evaluate the line integral of \mathbf{F} over the given path:
\mathbf{F} = \left\lt y,x\right> , \quad \varphi(x,y)=\frac1{1}x^{1}y^{1} ;
Upper half of a circle with radius 18, centered at the origin and oriented counterclockwise
Answer :

static.solution:
\varphi ( x,y )=\frac1{1}x^{1}y^{1}: \nabla \varphi = \left\lt \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial x},\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial y} \right> = \left\lt y, x \right> =\mathbf{F} We now use the Fundamental Theorem of Gradient Vector Fields.
The terminal point is Q=( -18,0 ) and the initial point is P=( 18,0 ), therefore: \int_{\mathbf{c}} \mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{s} = \varphi (Q)-\varphi (P)=\varphi ( -18,0 )-\varphi ( 18,0 )= \frac1{1}\cdot (-18)^{1}\cdot 0^{1}-\frac1{1}\cdot 18^{1}\cdot 0^{1} = 0

statement.p: Determine whether the vector field is conservative and, if so, find the general potential function.
Note: if the vector field is not conservative, write "DNE".

static.solution:
\mathbf{F} satisfies the cross partials condition: \begin{array}{l}\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial }{\partial y}( \cos z )=0\\ \frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial }{\partial x}( 2 y^{19} )=0\end{array} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial x} \begin{array}{rcl}\frac{\partial F_2}{\partial z}=\frac{\partial }{\partial z}( 2 y^{19} )=0\\ \frac{\partial F_3}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial }{\partial y}( -x \sin z )=0\end{array} \Rightarrow \frac{\partial F_2}{\partial z}=\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial y}\begin{array}{rcl}\frac{\partial F_3}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial }{\partial x}( -x \sin z )=- \sin z\\ \frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z}=\frac{\partial }{\partial z}( \cos z )=- \sin z\end{array} \Rightarrow \frac{\partial F_3}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial F_1}{\partial z} We see that the conditions are satisfied, therefore \mathbf{F} is conservative. We find the general potential function for \mathbf{F}.
Step 1. Use the condition \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial x}= F_1.
\varphi ( x,y,z ) is an antiderivative of F_1= \cos z when y and z are fixed, therefore: \varphi ( x,y,z )=\int \cos z \,dx=x \cos z+g( y,z ) \quad \mathbf{(1)} Step 2. Use the condition \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial y}= F_2.
Using \mathbf{(1)} we get: \frac{\partial }{\partial y}\left(x \cos z+g( y,z )\right) = 2 y^{19} g_y(y,z) = 2 y^{19} We integrate with respect to y, holding z fixed: g(y,z)=\int 2 y^{19} \,dy= \frac1{10} \cdot y^{20} + g(z) Substituting in \mathbf{(1)} gives \varphi(x,y,z)=x \cos z+ \frac{y^{20}}{10}+g(z)\quad \mathbf{(2)} Step 3. Use the condition \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial z}= F_3.
By \mathbf{(2)} we have \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\left(x \cos z+ \frac{y^{20}}{10}+g(z)\right) = -x \sin z -x \sin z+ g'(z) = -x \sin z g'(z) = 0\quad\Rightarrow\quad g(z)=c Substituting in \mathbf{(2)} we obtain the general potential function: \varphi ( x,y,z )=x \cos z+ \frac{y^{20}}{10}+c

static.solution: (a) We substitute x=6 t, y=3 t, z=2 t in the function f( x,y,z )=x+yz to find f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right): f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right)=6 t+( 3 t )( 2 t )=6 t+6 t^2 We differentiate the vector \mathbf{c}(t) and compute the length of the derivative vector: {\mathbf{c}}'(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\left\lt 6 t,3 t,2 t \right> = \left\lt 6,3,2 \right>\quad\Rightarrow\quad {\| \mathbf{c}}'(t) \|=\sqrt{{6}^2+ {3}^2+ {2}^2}=\sqrt{49} Hence, ds=\| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\| \,dt=\sqrt{49} \,dt (b) Computing the scalar line integral, we obtain \int_{\mathcal{C}} f( x,y,z ) \,ds =\int_0^1 f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right)\| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\| \,dt =\int_0^1 (6t+6t^{2})\cdot \sqrt{49} \,dt= \sqrt{49}\left(3 t^2+\frac{6}3 t^3\right)\bigg|_0^1 =\sqrt{49}\left(3+\frac{6}3\right)= \frac{15 \sqrt{49}}{3} \approx 35

statement.p: Calculate the integral of f(x,y,z) = 8 x^2+8 y^2+z^{9} over the curve \mathbf{c}(t) = (\cos t, \sin t, t) for 0\le t\le \pi.

static.solution:
[Step 1.] Compute \|\mathbf{c}'(t)\|.
We differentiate \mathbf{c}(t): \mathbf{c}'(t)=\frac{d}{dt} \left\lt \cos t,\sin t,t \right> = \left\lt -\sin t,\cos t,1 \right> Hence, \|\mathbf{c}'(t)\| = \sqrt{(-\sin t)^2+\cos^2t+1^2} = \sqrt{\sin^2t+\cos^2t+1} = \sqrt{2} \,ds = \|\mathbf{c}'(t)\| \,dt=\sqrt{2} \,dt [Step 2.] Write out f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right).
We substitute x=\cos t, y=\sin t, z=t in f(x,y,z)= 8 x^2+8 y^2+z^{9} to obtain f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right)=8 \cos^2t+8 \sin^2t+t^{9}=8+ t^{9} [Step 3.] Compute the line integral.
Using the Theorem on Scalar Line Integrals we obtain \int_{\mathcal{C}} (8 x^2+8 y^2+z^{9}) \,ds = \int_0^{\pi} f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right)\|\mathbf{c}'(t)\| \,dt = \int_0^{\pi} (8+ t^{9})\sqrt{2} \,dt =\sqrt{2}\left(8 t+\frac{t^{10} }{10}\right)\bigg|_0^{\pi} = \sqrt{2}\left(8 \pi+\frac{\pi^{10} }{10}\right)

statement.p: Compute the line integral of the scalar function f(x,y)= \sqrt{1+9xy}
over the curve y=x^3 for 0\le x \le 9

static.solution:
\mathbf{c}(t)=\left(t, t^3\right) for 0\le t\le 9
[Step 1.] Compute \| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\|.
We have {\mathbf{c}}'(t)=\frac{\,d}{\,dt}\left\lt t, t^3 \right> = \left\lt 1,3 t^2 \right> \quad\Rightarrow\quad \| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\| =\sqrt{1+9 t^4} [Step 2.] Write out f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right).
We substitute x=t, y= t^3 in f( x,y )=\sqrt{1+9xy} to obtain f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right)=\sqrt{1+9t\cdot t^3}=\sqrt{1+9 t^4} [Step 3.] Compute the line integral.
We use the Theorem on Scalar Line Integrals to write \int_{\mathcal{C}} f( x,y ) \,ds = \int_0^{9} f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right)\| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\| \,dt=\int_0^{9} \sqrt{1+9 t^4}\sqrt{1+9 t^4} \,dt= \int_0^{9} \left(1+9 t^4\right) \,dt=t+\frac{9 t^5}{5}\bigg|_0^{9}=\frac{531486}{5}=106297

statement.p: Compute the line integral of the scalar function f(x,y,z)= 2x^2+8z
over the curve \mathbf{c}(t)=(e^t,t^2,t) \text{,} \quad 0\le t\le 1

static.solution:
[Step 1.] Compute \| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\|.
{\mathbf{c}}'(t)= \frac{\,d}{\,dt}\left\lt e^t , t^2,t \right> = \left\lt e^t ,2t,1 \right> \quad\Rightarrow\quad \| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\| =\sqrt{e^{2t}+4 t^2+1} [Step 2.] Write out f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right).
We substitute x= e^t, y= t^2, z=t in f( x,y,z )=2 x^2+8z to obtain: f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right)=2 e^{2t}+8t [Step 3.] Compute the line integral.
We have \int_{\mathcal{C}} f( x,y,z ) \,ds =\int_0^{1} f\left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right)\| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\| \,dt = \int_0^{1} (2 e^{2t}+8t)\sqrt{e^{2t}+4 t^2+1} \,dt We compute the integral using the substitution u={e^{2t}+4 t^2+1}, du=\left({2 e^{2t}+8t}\right) \,dt. We get: \int_{\mathcal{C}} f( x,y,z ) \,ds = \int_2^{e^{2}+5} u^{1/2} \,du= \frac23 u^{3/2}\bigg|_2^{e^{2}+5}= \frac23\left({(e^{2}+5)}^{3/2}-2^{3/2}\right)

statement.p: Calculate the total mass of a circular piece of wire of radius 3 cm centered at the origin whose mass density is \rho(x,y)=x^2~\mathrm{g/cm}.
Answer : \mathrm{g}

static.solution: M=\int_{\mathcal{C}} x^2 \,ds We use the following parametrization of the wire: \mathbf{c}(t)=( 3 \cos t, 3 \sin t ),\quad 0\le t\le 2\pi Hence, {\mathbf{c}}'(t)= \left\lt -3 \sin t,\,3 \cos t \right> \quad\Rightarrow\quad \| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\| =\sqrt{{( -3 \sin t )}^2+{( 3 \cos t )}^2}=3 We compute the line integral using the Theorem on Scalar Line Integrals. We get M = \int_0^{2\pi } \rho \left(\mathbf{c}(t)\right)\| {\mathbf{c}}'(t)\| \,dt= \int_0^{2\pi } {( 3 \cos t )}^2\cdot 3 \,dt= 27\int_0^{2\pi } \cos^2t \,dt=27\left(\frac{t}{2}+\frac{\sin 2t}{4}\right)\bigg|_0^{2\pi }=27\cdot \frac{2\pi }{2}=27\pi \mathrm{g}

statement.p: (a) What is the direction of rotation of a thin twig placed at the origin along the x-axis?
(b) What is the direction of rotation of a thin twig placed at the origin along the y-axis?
(c) If we put a paddle wheel at the origin, instead of a twig, in what direction would you expect that to rotate?
(d) Compute curl \vec F.

static.solution:
(a) A thin twig at the origin along the x-axis would only feel the velocity perpendicular to that axis, and thus would rotate in a clockwise direction.
(b) Similarly, if oriented along the y-axis, rotate in a counterclockwise direction.
(c) Combining (a) and (b), we expect the paddle wheel will not rotate.
(d) Using the Cartesian coordinate definition, we get \mbox{curl} \vec F=\left |\begin{array}{ccc}\vec i\amp \vec j\amp \vec k\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\amp \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\amp \frac{\partial}{\partial z}\\ (-x-y) \amp (-x) \amp 0\end{array}\right | = \boldsymbol{0}. This is as expected, since a paddle-wheel (instead of a twig) placed in the field would behave as indicated in (c).

Three small squares, S_1, S_2, and S_3, each with side 0.1 and centered at the point (8, 6, 1), lie parallel to the xy-, yz- and xz-planes, respectively. The squares are oriented counterclockwise when viewed from the positive z-, x-, and y-axes, respectively. A vector field \vec G has circulation around S_1 of -2, around S_2 of -0.04, and around S_3 of -4. Estimate curl \vec G at the point (8, 6, 1)

static.solution:
\vec G has its component in the x-direction given by (\mbox {curl }\vec G)_x \approx \frac{\mbox {Circulation around small square around } x \mbox {-axis}}{\mbox {Area inside square}} = \frac{\mbox {Circulation around }S_2}{\mbox {Area inside }S_2}= \frac{-0.04}{(0.1)^2} = -4. Similar reasoning leads to (\mbox {curl }\vec G)_y\approx \frac{\mbox {Circulation around } S_3}{\mbox {Area inside }S_3}=\frac{-4}{(0.1)^2}=-400. and (\mbox {curl }\vec G)_z\approx\frac{\mbox {Circulation around } S_1}{\mbox {Area inside }S_1}=\frac{-2}{(0.1)^2}=-200.
Thus, \mbox {curl }\vec G\approx -4\,\mathit{\vec i}-400\,\mathit{\vec j}-200\,\mathit{\vec k}.

statement.p: A horizontal square has sides of 1400 km running north-south and east-west. A wind blows from the west and increases in magnitude toward the north at a rate of 8 m/s for every 700 km. Compute the circulation of the wind counterclockwise around the square.
circulation =

p.em: (Include .)

static.solution:
v meter/sec on the south side and (v + 16) meter/sec on the north side.
The circulation is the sum of the line integrals along the four sides of the square. The line integrals along the eastern and western edges are both zero, since the wind velocity is perpendicular to these edges. The integral to the right along the south side equals (1400\mbox{ km})(- v \mbox{ m/s})= - 1.4 v \times 10^{6} \mbox{ m}^2/\mbox{s}, and the integral to the left along the north side equals (-1400\mbox{ km})(-(v + 16) \mbox{ m/s}) = 1.4(v + 16) \times 10^{6} \mbox{ m}^2/\mbox{s}. The total circulation is then the sum of these, \mbox{circulation} = -1.4 v \times 10^{6} + 1.4(v + 16) \times 10^{6} = -2.24 \times 10^{7} \mbox{ m}^2/\mbox{s}.

statement.p: Let \mbox{curl }\vec F = -2y\,\mathit{\vec i}+3z\,\mathit{\vec j}-3\,\mathit{\vec k}, let P =(2,4,3), and let C be the circle of radius 0.005 centered at P in the plane x+y+z = 9, oriented clockwise when viewed from the origin.
(a) Find \mbox{curl }\vec F\cdot(\vec i+\vec j+\vec k) at P.
(b) Use your answer to part (a) to estimate \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r.

static.solution:
(a) At P, we have \mbox{curl } \vec F = -8\,\mathit{\vec i}+9\,\mathit{\vec j}-3\,\mathit{\vec k}, so \mbox{curl }\vec F\cdot(\vec i+\vec j+\vec k) = (-8) + (9) + (-3) = -2.
(b) The definition of the curl tells us that if \vec n is the unit vector normal to the plane containing the circle and pointing away from the origin, then \mbox{curl } \vec F\cdot\vec n\approx \frac{\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r}{\hbox{Area enclosed by }C}. Since \vec n=(\vec i+\vec j+\vec k)/\sqrt 3, we have \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r\approx (\mbox{curl }\vec F \cdot\vec n)(\mbox{Area of circle}) = \frac{-2}{\sqrt 3}\pi(0.005)^2 = -9.069\times 10^{-5}.

statement.p: A vortex that rotates at constant angular velocity w about the z-axis has velocity vector field \vec v = w(-y \vec i + x \vec j).

(a) Sketch, on a separate sheet of paper, the vector field with w = 1 and the vector field with w = -1. Then determine the speed \Vert{\vec v}\Vert of the vortex as a function of the distance from its center, r.
speed =
(b) Compute \mbox{div } \vec v and \mbox{curl } \vec v.
(c) Compute the circulation of \vec v counterclockwise about the circle of radius R in the xy-plane, centered at the origin.
circulation =

static.solution:
(a) Cross sections of the vector fields are shown below, for w = 1 on the left and for w = -1 on the right. In either case the cross-section is taken in the xy-plane and vectors are drawn with a dot at the tail of each vector.
w = 1 w = -1
The distance from the center of the vortex is given by r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}. The velocity of the vortex at any point is -w y\vec i + w x\vec j, and the speed of the vortex at any point is the magnitude of the velocity, or s=\Vert{\vec {v}}\Vert=\sqrt{(-w y)^2+(w x)^2} =\left|w \right| \sqrt{x^2 + y^2} = \left| w\right| r.
(b) The divergence of the velocity field is given by: \mbox{div } \vec v = \frac{\partial (-w y)}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial w x}{\partial y} = 0. The curl of the field is: \mbox{curl } \vec{v} = \mbox{curl} (-w y\vec i + w x\vec j) = \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x} \left( w x\right) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( -w y\right) \right)\vec k = 2w \vec k
(c) We know that \vec{v} has constant magnitude | w | R everywhere on the circle and is everywhere tangential to the circle. In addition, if w > 0, the vector field rotates counterclockwise; if w \lt 0, the vector field rotates clockwise. Thus if w > 0, \vec{v} and d\vec{r} are parallel and in the same direction, so \int_C \vec{v}\cdot d{\vec{r}} = \left| \vec{v}\right| \cdot \left( \mbox{Length of }C \right) = w R\cdot 2\pi R = 2\pi w R^2. If w \lt 0, then \left| w \right| =-w and \vec{v} and d \vec{r} are in opposite directions, so \int_C \vec{v}\cdot {d\vec{r}} = -\left| \vec{v}\right| \cdot \left( \mbox{Length of }C \right) = -\left| w \right| R\cdot \left( 2\pi R\right) = 2\pi w R^2.

statement.p: Calculate \int_C \left(8 (x^2-y)\vec i + 2(y^2+x)\vec j\right) \cdot d\vec r if:
(a) C is the circle (x-2)^2+(y-1)^2=1 oriented counterclockwise.
(b) C is the circle (x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=R^2 in the xy-plane oriented counterclockwise.

static.solution:
(a) The curve, C, is closed and oriented in the correct direction for Green's Theorem. Writing A for the interior of the circle, we have \int_C \left( 8(x^2-y)\vec i +2(y^2+x)\vec j\right)\cdot d\vec r = \int_A \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}2 (y^2+x) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}8(x^2-y)\right) dx\,dy = \int_A (2-(-8))\, dx\,dy = 10 \int_A dx\,dy = 10\cdot \mbox{Area of }A = 10\pi.
(b) The circle given has radius R and center (a,b). The argument in part (a) works for any circle of radius R, oriented counterclockwise. So the line integral has the value 10\pi R^2.

statement.p: Let \vec F = 12 x e^{y}\,\vec i + 6 x^2 e^{y}\,\vec j and \vec G = 12(x - y)\,\vec i + 6(x + y)\,\vec j. Let C be the path consisting of lines from (0,0) to (3,0) to (3,4) to (0,0). Find each of the following integrals exactly:

static.solution:
(a) Since \vec F = 12 x e^{y}\,\vec i + 6 x^2 e^{y}\,\vec j is a gradient vector field and C is a closed curve, \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = 0.
(b) Since \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(6(x + y)) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(12(x - y)) = 18, by Green's Theorem,\int_C\vec G\cdot d\vec r = \int_R\left(18\right)\,dA = 18(\mbox{Area of triangle}) = 108.

statement.p: Let \vec F = (3 x^2 y + y^3 + 5 e^x)\,\vec i + (3 e^{y^2} + 48 x)\,\vec j. Consider the line integral of \vec F around the circle of radius a, centered at the origin and traversed counterclockwise.
(a) Find the line integral for a=1.
line integral =
(b) For which value of a is the line integral a maximum?

p.em: (Be sure you can explain why your answer gives the correct maximum.)

static.solution:
(a) We use Green's Theorem. Let R be the region enclosed by the circle C. Then \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_R\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(3 e^{y^2} + 48 x) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(3 x^2 y + y^3 + 5 e^x)\right)\,dA = \int_R 48 - 3(x^2 + y^2)\, dA. Converting to polar coordinates, we have \int_C \vec F\cdot d\vec r = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 (48 - 3 r^2)r\,dr\,d\theta = 2\pi\left(24 r^2 - \frac{3}{4} r^4\right)\bigg|_0^1 = \frac{93}{2}\pi.
(b) The integrand of the integral over the disk R is 48 - 3(x^2+y^2). Since the integrand is positive for x^2 + y^2 \lt \frac{48}{3} = 16 and negative for x^2 + y^2 > 16, the integrand is positive inside the circle of radius 4 and negative outside that circle. Thus, the integral over R increases with a until a=4 and then decreases. The maximum value of the line integral occurs when a = 4.

(b) Parameterizing the unit circle, C, by x=\cos t, y=\sin t, 0\le t\le 2\pi, we have \vec r'(t) =-\sin t\,\vec i+ \cos t\,\vec j, so \int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r = 2\int_0^{2\pi}((\sin t)\vec i+(\cos t)\vec j)\cdot ((-\sin t)\vec i+(\cos t)\vec j)\,dt = 2\int_0^{2\pi}\cos (2t)\,dt = 0. statement.p: Use Green's Theorem to evaluate the line integral \oint_{\mathcal{C}} y^{4}\,dx + x^{2}\,dy
where \mathcal{C} is the boundary of the square -1\le x \le 1, -1\le y \le 1 oriented counterclockwise.

static.solution:
We have P= y^{4} and Q= x^{2}, therefore \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=2x-4y^{3} Using Green's Theorem we obtain \int_{\mathcal{C}} y^{4} \,dx+ x^{2} \,dy = \iint_{\mathcal{D}}\left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right) \,dA= \iint_{\mathcal{D}} (2x-4y^{3}) \,dx \,dy =2\iint_{\mathcal{D}} x \,dx \,dy-4\iint_{\mathcal{D}} y^{3} \,dx \,dy By symmetry, the positive and negative values of x cancel each other in the first integral, so this integral is zero.
The second double integral is zero by similar reasoning. Therefore, \int_{\mathcal{C}} y^{4} \,dx+ x^{2} \,dy=0-0=0

static.solution:
z=6\sqrt{x-1}, 1\le x\le 2, around the z-axis is shown in the figure below.
At height z, the cross-section is a horizontal circle of radius a. Thus, letting the angle \theta around the z-axis be t, a point on this horizontal circle is given by \vec r=a \cos t \vec i + a \sin t \vec j + z\vec k. However, the radius a and height z are not independent. We can parameterize easily in two ways: first, suppose that we take the radius a to be our second parameter, a = s. Then, the height z = 6\sqrt{s - 1}, and our parameterization is x(s,t) = s\cos t, y(s,t) = s\sin t, and z(s,t) = 6\sqrt{s - 1}, with 1\le s\le 2 \quad\mbox{and}\quad 0\le t\le 2\pi. Alternately, we could take the height z to be the second parameter, z = s. Then, solving for the radius r in the expression for the curve, we get a = \left(\frac{s}{6}\right)^2 + 1. Thus in this case the parameterization is x(s,t) = \left((\frac{s}{6})^2 + 1\right)\,\cos(t), y(s,t) = \left((\frac{s}{6})^2 + 1\right)\,\sin(t), and z(s,t) = s, with 0\le s\le 6\quad\mbox{and}\quad 0\le t\le 2\pi.

static.solution:
(a) Let z be measured from the bottom of the post, and the center of the post be at x = 0, y = 0. The surface is the revolution surface obtained by revolving a curve extending vertically along one edge of the surface around the z axis, as suggested by the figure below.
From the measurements given, we obtain the equation of the curve x = \cos \left( \frac{\pi}{6} z \right) + 3, \qquad 0 \leq z \leq 72.
Rotating this around the z-axis, taking z=s and \theta = t as the parameters, we get the parametric equations x = (\cos \left( \frac{\pi}{6} s \right)+3)\cos t, y = (\cos \left( \frac{\pi}{6} s \right)+3)\sin t, and z = s, with 0 \leq s \leq 72, \qquad 0 \leq t \leq 2\pi.
(b) We know that the points in the curve consists of cross-sections of circles parallel to the xy plane and of radius \cos((\pi/{6})z+3). Thus, \mbox{Area of cross-section} = \pi\left(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{6}z+3\right)\right)^2 Integrating over z, we get \hbox{Volume } = \pi \int_0^{72} \left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6} z+3\right)^2 dz = \pi \int_0^{72} \left(\cos^2\frac{\pi}{6}z+6\cos\frac{\pi}{6}z +9 \right) dz = 684 \pi \mbox{ in}^3.

The projection of the cone onto the yz-plane is obtained by setting x=0 in the equation of the cone, that is, x=0=\sqrt{z^2- y^2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad z=\pm y Since on S, z\ge 0, we get z=|y|. We conclude that the projection of the upper part of the cone x^2+y^2=z^2 onto the yz-plane is
the region between the lines z=y and z=-y on the upper part of the yz-plane.
Therefore, the projection \mathcal{D} of S onto the yz-plane is the region shown in the figure:
With r_0=8
The area of S is the surface integral: \mathrm{Area}(S)=\iint_S \,dS We compute the integral using a surface integral over a graph. Since x=g(y,z)=\pm\sqrt{z^2-y^2} we have, g_z=\pm \frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2- y^2}}, \, g_y =\pm \frac{y}{\sqrt{z^2-y^2}} Hence, (notice that z\ge 0 on S): \sqrt{1+ g_y^2+g_z^2} = \sqrt{1+\frac{z^2}{z^2-y^2}+\frac{y^2}{z^2-y^2}} =\sqrt{\frac{2z^2}{z^2-y^2}} = \frac{z\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{z^2-y^2}} We obtain the following integral: \mathrm{Area}(S) =\iint_{\mathcal{D}} \sqrt{1+ g_y^2+ g_z^2} \,dy \,dz= \iint_{\mathcal{D}} \frac{z\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{z^2- y^2}} \,dz \,dy Using symmetry gives: \mathrm{Area}(S) = 4 \int_0^{8/(\sqrt{2})} \int_y^{\sqrt{64-y^2}} \frac{z\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{z^2- y^2}} \,dz \,dy=4\sqrt{2} \int_0^{8/(\sqrt{2})} \left(\int_y^{\sqrt{64- y^2}} \frac{z \,dz}{\sqrt{z^2- y^2}}\right) \,dy \quad \mathbf{(1)} We compute the inner integral using the substitution u=\sqrt{z^2-y^2}, \,du=\frac zu\,dz. We get: \int_y^{\sqrt{64-y^2}} \frac{z\,dz}{\sqrt{z^2-y^2}} = \int_0^{\sqrt{64-2y^2}} \frac{u\,du}{u} =\int_0^{\sqrt{64-2y^2}}\,du=\sqrt{64-2y^2} We substitute in \mathbf{(1)} and compute the resulting integral using the substitution t=\frac1{8}\sqrt{2}y. We get: \mathrm{Area}(S) = 4\sqrt{2} \int_0^{8/(\sqrt{2})} \sqrt{64-2 y^2} \,dy=4\sqrt{2} \int_0^1 \sqrt{64-64 t^2} \frac{8 dt}{\sqrt{2}}=4\cdot {8}^2\int_0^1 \sqrt{1- t^2}\,dt= 4\cdot {8}^2\cdot \frac{\pi}{4}= 64 \pi

static.solution:
S is parameterized by \vec r(r,\theta)=r\cos \theta\vec i+r\sin \theta\vec j+r\vec k, with 0\le r\le R and 0\le\theta\le 2\pi. We have \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial r}\times \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial \theta} = \left|\begin{array}{ccc} \vec i \amp \vec j \amp \vec k\\ \cos{\theta} \amp \sin{\theta} \amp 1 \\ -r\sin{\theta} \amp r\cos{\theta} \amp 0 \end{array}\right| = - r \cos\theta \vec i - r \sin \theta \vec j + r \vec k. Since the vector \partial \vec r / \partial r \times \partial \vec r / \partial \theta points upward, in the direction opposite to the specified orientation, we use d\vec A= -\left(\partial\vec r/\partial r\times\partial\vec r/\partial\theta\right) \,dr\,d\theta = (r\cos\theta\vec i + r\sin\theta\vec j - r\vec k)\, dr\,d\theta\,.
Hence \int_S\vec F\cdot d\vec A = \int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^R 8 (r^5 \cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta\vec k)\cdot (r \cos\theta \vec i + r \sin \theta \vec j - r \vec k)\,dr\,d\theta = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{R} -8 r^6\cos^2{\theta}\sin^2{\theta}\,dr\,d\theta = -\frac{8 R^7}{7}\int_0^{2\pi} \sin^2{\theta}\cos^2{\theta}\, d\theta = -\frac{8 R^7}{7}\int_0^{2\pi} \sin^2{\theta}(1-\sin^2{\theta})\, d\theta = -\frac{ 8 R^7}{7}\int_0^{2\pi} (\sin^2{\theta}-\sin^4{\theta})\, d\theta = -\left(\frac{8 R^7}{7}\right)\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)= -\frac{2}{7} \pi R^7.
The cone is not differentiable at the point (0,0). However the flux integral, which is improper, converges.

statement.p: Compute the flux of the vector field \vec F = z\vec i + 8 x\vec j through the parameterized surface S oriented upward and given, for 0\le s\le 4, \ \ 2\le t\le 4, by x=s^2, \quad y=2s+t^2, \quad z=6 t.
flux =

static.solution:
\partial \vec r / \partial s \times \partial \vec r / \partial t is given by \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial s}\times\frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial t}= \left|\begin{array}{ccc} \quad\vec i\quad\amp \quad\vec j\quad\amp \quad\vec k\quad\\ 2s \amp 2 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 2t \amp 6 \end{array} \right| = 12\vec i- 12 s\vec j+4st\vec k. Since the z-component, 4st, of the vector \partial \vec r / \partial s \times \partial \vec r / \partial t is positive for 0 \lt s \leq 4, 2 \leq t \leq 4, we see that \partial \vec r/\partial s \times \partial \vec r / \partial t points upward, in the direction of the orientation of S we were given.
Thus, we use d\vec A = \left(\frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial s} \times \frac{\partial \vec r}{\partial t}\right)\,ds\,dt, and so we have \int_S\vec F\cdot d\vec A = \int_0^{4}\int_{2}^{4} (6 t\vec i + 8 s^2\vec j)\cdot (12\vec i- 12 s\vec j+4st\vec k)\,dt\,ds =\int_0^{4}\int_{2}^{4} (72 t - 96 s^3)\,dt\,ds = \int_0^{4}(36 t^2 - 96 s^3 t)\bigg|_{t=2}^{t=4}\,ds =\int_0^{4}(432 - 192 s^3)\,ds=(432s - 48 s^4)\bigg|_0^{4} =-10560.

statement.p: Are the following statements true or false?

li.p: If S is the unit sphere centered at the origin, oriented outward and the flux integral \displaystyle \iint_S \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{A} is zero, then \vec{F} = \vec{0}.
If S is an open-ended circular cylinder centered about the z-axis, oriented away from the z-axis, and \vec{F} = \langle x,y,0 \rangle, then the flux of \vec{F} through S is positive.
If S is an open-ended circular cylinder centered about the z-axis, oriented away from the z-axis, and \vec{F} = \langle 3,-2,6 \rangle, then the flux of \vec{F} through S is zero.

If S is the unit sphere centered at the origin, oriented outward and the flux integral \displaystyle \iint_S \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{A} is zero, then \vec{F}(x,y,z) is perpendicular to \vec{r} = \langle x,y,z \rangle at every point of S.
The area vector of a flat, oriented surface is parallel to the surface.

If S is the unit sphere centered at the origin, oriented outward and \vec{F} = x \vec{i} + y \vec{j} + z\vec{k} = \vec{r}, then the flux integral \displaystyle \iint_S \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{A} is positive.
If S is the cube bounded by the six planes x = \pm 3, y = \pm 3, z = \pm 3, oriented outward, and \vec{F} = 2 \vec{i} - \vec{k}, then the flux of \vec{F} through S is zero.
